When this item was under discussion yesterday, the engineering aspect of the matter was discussed by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), the minister and myself, and possibly the item would have been passed without very much further discussion had not the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) seen fit to interject into the discussion his old speeches of three or four years ago when he was finding fault with the classification. Every member of this House who was here from 1906 to 1911 will remember all the old stock arguments about improper and dishonest classifications taking place on the Transcontinental. The hon. member for St. Antoine yesterday said that there had been sympathetic

classifications, which I understood him to define as being classifications made over and above what they should be in.order to help out the contractor. I would prefer that the hon. gentleman should use a term which everybody can understand, and not one which conveys the meaning in covered language. If an engineer classifies a cut differently from what it ought to be, it is not a sympathetic, but a dishonest classification; therefore, my hon. friend makes the charge that dishonest classification is the cause of the cost of this road exceeding the amount which he said was estimated in the beginning. It is true that at one time the late Minister of Finance did say in his judgment, or in the judgment of the engineers, this work was going to cost about $56,000,000, and it will now cost, according to the statements given by the minister yesterday, $162,000,000. But no one knows better than the hon. member for St. Antoine that that .statement was rrsade before the work was commenced, before a sod had been turned or a cubic yard of material was removed. It was clearly an estimate, based not upon an investigation of the country, but purely on the general principle contained in the assertion; You can build a road through Canada for so many thousand dollars a mile, therefore this road is going to cost so many millions. When the engineers were put on the work, they found greater difficulties than had been expected, it but was not the difficulties encountered that resulted in the increased cost of the road; it was the fact that the Government determined to build such a road as had never been built in Canada before, such a road as had never been built in America before and probably was not to be equalled by a road of so great a length in any place in the world.
My hon. friend said he had gone with his pick and shovel down to New Brunswick,^ just as he had gone to the West with his little kodak, taking pictures and then 'going around with his magic lantern endeavouring to make the people of Canada believe that there was something crooked in connection with the	Department of the Interior in the management of	public	lands. Even
*that did not land1 him in the Government, and now he goes around with his nick and shovel to see if he can do something with the Transcontinental. It is just the interposition of such persons as my hon. friend the member for St. Antoine with his little pick that is causing all the trouble in the Transcontinental to-day. He says he dug into the side of a cut, and was satisfied Mr. CAE YELL.
that it was not classified properly. It is just because the minister's inspecting engineers are doing the very same thing the hon. member for St. Antoine did that he is not getting from them the reports he ought to get. My hon. friend himself is engineer enough, without consulting anybody else, to know that if he goes to a cut after it has been exposed to the action of the weather for three or four years, he cannot tell by the use of a little pick what the nature of the cut actually was when it was first made. It is not difficult .for any man to classify a solid ledge cut, rock from top to bottom, but I do not think my hon. friend the member for St. Antoine can tell by going into an ordinary cut with a pick whether in its natural state it could have been ploughed with a team of six horses. There may be a few inches on the surface which, having been exposed to the elements during a period of four years, can be turned with a pick and ploughed with a taem of six horses, but that is not saying that that was the case when the cut was made, and it is not saying that the cut should have been classified as 50 per cent loose rock or 30 per cent loose rock. The best engineer my hon. friend can send does not possess the knowledge of the man who was there when the work was done.
The hon. minister started out to find a great big steal in connection with this matter. 1 have no doubt that many- of his friends believe that there has been a steal, as we do not disguise the fact that the cost of this road has been a great deal more than first estimated. My hon. friend sent out one engineer 'after another. I have not an accurate knowledge of anything west of Quebec, but I can tell my hon. friend that at least half a dozen different *sets of engineers have gone over that road from Moncton west for two or three hundred miles. When one set of engineers could not find anything to report that was against the management of the road, they sent another set, and they sent engineer after engineer to see if they could not disclose a steal, but they were unable to do so. When they could not find anything wrong, in order to justify their existence they had to commence cheese-paring. They would go into a out and sav: Well, if this was classified as 50 per cent loose rock, we will cut it down to 45 per cent. This they did without any reason and without any investigation, simply to justify their existence. The hon. member for St. Antoine yesterday tried to make us believe that the Government was saving millions of dollars by means of their inspecting engineers-engineers who have not even the good taste to work under the proper officials; engineers who were simply acting as pimps; men who are going around

without the knowledge of their superiors and reporting direct to the commissioner or to the minister; men who are simply hunting for mares' nests, and cannot find them. Let me tell you the result of what they have done in district A. According to the statement given to the House by the minister, the grading of district A has cost $8,319,000, clearing, $158,000, grubbing, $98,000, ballast and ballasting, $508,000! After investigating the matter for a year and ,a half, after sending set after set of engineers over this work to find something, my hon. friend was able to cut off about $17,000 from contract No. 1. I have not the exact figures, but I am approximately correct. On contract No. 2 they could not take off anything. On contracts 3 and 4, which were under the same management, they have taken off about $25,000. There is more than that in dispute, there is some question about extras, but, so far as the inspecting engineers are concerned, they have been able to cut off somewhere about $25,000. Contract No. 5 is the one referred to particularly by the hon. member for St. Antoine Division (Mr. Ames) as costing so much money, thirty-two miles costing $120,000 a mile. On that contract 5, they have not taken off more than $15,000 to $18,000 out of a three or four million dollar contract. They tried to and could not do it.
To show the minister that this is not a question of engineering, I will state what they have done on contract No. 5; that is the one that has been settled, and in that way I have been able to find out something about it. They started to cut off $30,000 or $35,000 and the company simply told them that they would not stand for it, because they were wrong, as no engineering judgment could say that they were entitled to make that reduction. They brought the manager of the company up here, and took him before the Star Chamber tribunal and examined him, put him on his oath, and brought all the engineers they could get from the province of New Brunswick, and put them under oath under this Star Chamber process. They could not justify anything that they had done, and the manager of the company simply told them he would fight them. Then they said: Let us settle this; we have taken off $25,000 from your classification, we will give back to you one-fourth of that if you will settle. There was a difference of about $8,000 or $10,000 over a concrete part of the work, and they gave back all that was claimed on the concrete except a mere bagatelle. There was a fight over another portion of the work which they had no Tight to take away, and they said: We will give that back to you; and they have given back to him everything except $15,000 or
$16,000. If my hon. friend's inspecting engineers were right, they should have stayed right, if they were justified in reporting that $35,000 should be taken from the contract they should have kept that amount back. Either they were right or they were wrong and now they are neither one nor the other, because they said they should take off $35,000 and they have it down to $16,000.
According to your own statement there is a saving of $18,000. I do not know anything about the case.

$18,000 saved? $18,000
stolen from the pockets of the contractors. If my hon. friend would take off everything coming to a contractor, he would say it was saved. Does my hon. friend want to save money in that way? Is that his ambition? I hope my hon. friend will not make use of a word like that again.
I think this is quite uncalled for, because the report is not in, and, as the hon. member for South Renfrew said yesterday, we cannot discuss it without the report.

I am taking the responsibility of telling my hon. friend what will be in that report, and if I am wrong my hon. friend can tell the public that the hon. member for Carleton does not know what he is talking about; but the hon member for Carleton will take the responsibility of standing by any fact he has given the minister to-day. I have given my hon. friend the result of this great steal they have found by investigating this work in New Brunswick.
On contract 6 they have taken off nothing so far. But my hon. friend does not tell the House that under the original contract there was provision that all this work must be investigated and must be inspected by Grand Trunk Pacific engineers, and during all the progress of this work the Grand Trunk Pacific inspecting engineers were on the work. No estimate could be paid or was paid until it was first agreed to and ratified by the Grand Trunk Pacific engineer, and when a dispute arose, as my hon. friend knows, the law provides for an arbitration board consisting of the chief engineer of the Transcontinental, the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and a third man to be appointed by the Chief Justice of Canada, in this case, Mr. Collingwood Schreiber. That arbitration 'board went over contract A, they went over every foot of the ground, they travelled from the Quebec boundary to Moncton and inspected cut after cut, and they took into consideration all the objections, some hundreds of them, that were made by the Grand Trunk Pacific engineer. The result of it all was that about $17,000



were taken off a certain cut in contract No.
6 near Edmunston, and that is the only change that was made in the classification of that work by the arbitration board authorized by statute to investigate it, and that was all decided before my hon. friend came into office. As a result of the decision of the hoard of arbitration appointed under the law, the contractors paid many of the su'b-contractors and the result has been that much of the money so taken off the contractors had been paid to the sub-contractors because the payment was authorized by the board of arbitrators created by statute. In that case the sub-contractor does not lose but the contractor does. I appeal to the minister, who, I think, would like to do what is right, if he feels that this is a business proposition-if he feels that spending $45,000, as he admits, in inspecting engineers in order to take off the trifling amounts I have mentioned, and take thern. off in the manner I have described, is a big manly position for the Department of Railways and Canals to take.
Neither the contractors, nor the sub-contractors, nor anyone else has appealed to me. I have had nothing to do with it; it has been settled with the commission.	-
My hon. friend need not try to get away from responsibilities in that way.
It is all right; if they think they are not being treated right, and do not think it worth while to bring it to my notice, I do not see what I have to do with it.

My hon. friend is the
official head of the department. My answer is, why do you have men in your employ so unfair that the contractors have to come to you?

I do not think we
have.	,

The ordinary public
thinks that the minister appoints officials over those important matters who are reasonable officials. They do not suppose that the contractors are driven to the minister. Of course, if the minister lays down the principle that in every case a contractor is dissatisfied he has a right to appeal to the minister, the minister's time will be well filled up.

Under the Act the
chief engineer finally approves of the esti-. mates, and we have not made any changes at all.
The one-man commission will not take the advice of the chief engineer on matters just like that.

I would like to know when it was refused.
Mr. CARVELL.

I will give a case It
was on contract No. 5 in District A. I have not the particulars before me, but in the schedule there was a price given for a timber-lined tunnel and a concrete-lined tunnel. There was a tunnel on Contract 5, six or seven hundred feet long at a certain price, and a auestion arose whether it was a timber-lined tunnel or a concrete-lined tunnel. It made a difference to the contractor. The sub-contractor claimed that it was one, and the engineer claimed that it was the other. It made a difference of $4,000 or $5,000 to the sub-contractor. There is a clause in the specification and contract which provides that all questions of engineering shall be decided by the chief engineer, whose decision is final, with no apneal. There is also a clause which provides that any dispute on matters of law. instead of going to the ordinary courts, shall go to the Exchequer Court of Canada. This became a question of law as to the proper interpretation of that schedule in that contract. It is not a question for the chief engineer to decide, or ratheT his decision is not final. The sub-contractor will not settle. The chief engineer wanted to leave the matter open so that if the subcontractor brought an action against the contractor and "succeeded, the contractor could bring an action against the Government in the Exchequer Court. But the one man commission would not allow that to be done, and the result was that the contractor who had contract 5 was compelled to settle with the department and take his chance of an action for $5,000 or $6,000 being brought against him by the sub-contractor. If the sub-contractor succeeds, 'as a matter of law, he has no recourse against the commission. That is an illustration of how the commissioner will not take the advice of his chief engineer. If my hon. friend wants moTe illustrations I can give them to him. He does not know what is going on in this one man commission, and I would advise him to investigate. I am pointing out some of the iniquities in the way in which this commission is being run. My hon. friend says we are saving $18,000 by reason of turning out the late commissioners and putting in a new set of officials. I think I am interesting my hon. friend.
I do not think so.
Who is he.
My hon. friend is talking about what he does not know, he is absolutely wrong. The commissioner acted on the advice and recommendation of the chief engineer.

My hon. friend will have an opportunity to explain. I am glad I am giving him something to explain.
354i

some of the things which my hon. fnend has been doing, and some of the grounds on which my hon. friend from St. Antoine charges that there was a sympathetic classification all along this work and that it was responsible for the increased price.
Now I come to district ' F.' Any hon. member who was here in 1907-1908 will remember the great outcry over the Hodgins enquiry, and will know something about the charges which were made against the late commission in regard to district ' F.' We were told that graft was rampant, that
the engineers were classifying common excavation as solid rock, and that there was the greatest steal going on that had ever been known in Canada by reason of this classification. Major Hodgins was here for three or four weeks, and undertook to show that there was illegal classification going on in Quebec. We all remember the collapse of the thing. When matters had been brought to the attention of Major Hodgins that he had not known before, he had to admit that: I am all wrong, the Quebec classification is all Tight; I have been misinformed, and therefore I withdraw my statements. Hon. gentlemen who were here at that time know all about this. 'Then we had that arbitration board going through district ' F,' but the difficulty that the arbitration board had to decide was not one of classification. The admitted that the classification was all right, but that the difficulty was as to the overbreak. I am not positive as to the figures, but I can give them practically correctly. The arbitrators recommended the taking away of about half a million dollars from a contractor on district ' F ' on account, very largely, of overbreak. I am told-I may be wrong, and if so I would like the minister to correct me-that this overbreak has since been changed to about $100,000.	.
All this talk that we have had in Canada for the last five or six years about graft being rampant on the Transcontinental railway has been boiled down to the fact that out contractors used too great a quantity of explosives in their work, and that they took out a little more rock than could honestly be considered as overbreak; that is the taking out of rock and the making of the cut wider than it should have been made, or the taking out of more material than should have been taken out, and the result was that the contractors were not allowed their pay for all the material actually taken out. A reasonable amount is usually allowed for overbreak, 10, 15 or 20 per cent, and the only thing that the commission could find in district ' F ' was that the engineers had allowed about $100,000 for overbreak that they ought not to have allowed in a work involving some millions of dollars for
grading alone. These are the things for which the minister has been appointing engineer after engineer to go all over this country, these are the things for which a staff of engineers has been going all over the country, and they have failed to find anything wrong, but in order to justify their existence they have taken a little off one contract here and a little off another contract there, or practically enough to pay the cost of the engineers and the commissions.
If my hon. friend the minister is gratified that he has accomplished something that will redound to the credit of the Conservative party, he is welcome to it. But in my opinion my hon. friend is not gratified at his performance. I give my hon. friend this much credit, that I do not believe that he ever intended that such a performance should have been carried out by those engineers who have been carrying it out. I think he has too much horse sense, too much honesty, for that, and I believe there is no man in Canada who is as sick or as disheartened over the whole thing as the minister is, and I further believe that if he had his way he would fire the whole bunch and put back in their positions the men who ran the business for five years honestly and efficiently. I do not believe the Minister of Railways really wanted these things to happen, but party exigencies demanded that a ' big time ' must be made over the Transcontinental railway. Every man who sat behind his leader, when they were in opposition, cried ' wolf, wolf ' every time the Transcontinental railway was mentioned for five years. They said that it meant that there was a big steal going on and every man believed that there was an election fund being taken out of it, every man believed that there was a crqoked transaction going on in Canada and I will admit that, these views having been expressed, they were compelled to do something. I wonder if the minister is satisfied with the results, I wonder if he would not like to have back the old men in whom he must have confidence because it has been proved that the work was honestly and efficiently managed by men who knew what they were doing, who could not be bribed, and who would not swerve from the straight and narrow path.
In so far as the degrading of this road in districts ' C ' and ' D ' are concerned, I think my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals feels exactly the same about it as he must feel about the success of his investigating engineers in New Brunswick and in district ' F '. He must feel that they are doing something which is not redounding to the benefit of the road, that they are doing that largely only to save a few thousand dollars which means
Mr. CARVELL.

that they are taking away from that road the distinction of feeing the one great road on the continent of America which has been built up to the very top of modem standards. I hope even at this late date that my hon. friend will see his way clear to abandon these unnecessary tactics and go back to the real, genuine plan, of building the road upon the lines which he found laid down when he came into office. Before this discussion was closed yesterday afternoon I asked my hon. friend if he would give us a statement of the saving that will be effected by means of the change in these grades. He was good enough to tell me privately, after the House rose, that he could not give it offhand, and I accepted his statement. But his engineers have had a night to think it over and I would like to have approximately what the saving in cost would be by reason of these changes- I do not mean to a word or a dollar, but I do think that the minister or his engineers might be able to give me a very close approximate estimate of what the cost will be.

I do not propose to go into the question which has been discussed by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Car-veil). The report, unfortunately, has not been sent in yet, and I take the same ground as that taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) yesterday, that it is not proper to discuss that report before it is brought in.
I am not discussing the report; I am giving the facts to the committee.

I know that, but when the report comes in will be the proper time to go into all these questions. The report will either justify or condemn what my hon. friend has been saying. With reference to the information he asked for yesterday as to the saving effected by the adoption of the balanced grade, the engineer says that he has men working on it, and I shall be very glad to hand it to the hon. gentleman when it is furnished to me.
Will I have the assurance of the minister that I can have that before parliament prorogues?
Yes.

The answer
which has been given by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals to the legitimate inquiry of my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), that he will get this information as to what will be the effect of the change of grades in decreasing the cost of the road, is certainly the most astounding that Parliament could, receive. When we heard last summer that the new Administration intended _ to change the character of that road as originally designed,
there was in the country a good deal of surprise and anxiety. This road was intended to be unique in that throughout its entire length from ocean to ocean it was to have grades of four-tenths of one per cent. It was a new venture, and I think it was -a wise venture. But, whether wise or unwise-I still maintain wise-the construction of the road had been carried on with that high standard in view. These grades had been applied from Moncton to Quebec, from lake Superior Junction to-Winnipeg, and from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean. That was to be the uniform character of the road. But we learned last summer all of a sudden that on the section between lake Superior Junction and Quebec there "was to be a change in the character of the road, and that the grades which had been specified, approved by both parties to the agreement, the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and maintained up to that time, were to be changed to what are now called momentum grades. The reason for the change given at that time was that it was for the sake of economy. It was said that the road was very expensive; and it is an expensive road; The matter was brought to the attention of my hon. friend when Parliament opened in November last, six months ago, and he has had since then to prepare his answer. Therefore we had reason to expect, when he came to ask for money to carry on these works, that we would be told what was to be the character of the changes and the reason for them. We have not yet had a word of information as to the nature of the changes, where they are to be, and what their cost is to be. The only information we have on the matter is what the ex-M'in-ister of Railways (Mr. Graham) has been able to give us. Are we to understand, as has been stated, that, although these changes have been made for the sake of economy, the Government have gone into them without getting an estimate of foe cost? What is the result? To-day we have no figures at all. The changes were decided on more than twelve months ago. The work went on all through last summer, and the Government tell us to-day, without any hesitation, that they have no information to give; that they are making the changes blindly without information, and without looking to the consequences of their action. This is the result of want of information on the part o'f the hon. minister in charge. He tells us to-day that he does not know what ecofiomy he intends to practice. The only information we received from him yesterday was that there was a divided opinion as to the result of these changes, some engineers contending that momentum grades are better, in so far as the operation of the railway is concerned, than level .roads. I am not an engineer nor a railway man; but

anybody with common sense will understand that this statement will not hold water. Men can have different opinions on the subject, but nobody can persuade a man of common sense that momentum grades are better than level grades. The same thing is true as regards highways. By substituting momentum grades for level grades you degrade the road; it is less efficient. A still worse feature of the matter is that you have gone blindly into the change, and the correspondence which has been laid before the House makes the matter ten times worse. The contract provides that all specifications are to be made jointly by the Government engineer and the engineer of the Grand Trunk Eailway Company. When Mr. Chamberlin was informed of the changes which had taken place, he immediately and very properly applied for information to the commissioner, Major Leonard. My friend the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) read the correspon-' dence to the House yesterday. It is well that we should go over it again, in order to see the plain points which are involved in it, and which make the position of Major Leonard and of the Government almost intolerable. This is the first letter of Mr. Chamberlin:
I learn from our engineers that the standard of work on that portion of the Transcontinental railway between Lake Superior Junction and Cochrane, which was at the outset adopted and has so far been complied with, is being departed from, and that instead of four-tenths .grade and permanent structures, you have authorized grades up to One per cent and the erection of temporary wooden structures. In regard to this I would call attention to clause 7 of this agreement of the 29th July, 1903, which provides that the work of construction of the eastern division shall be done according to the specifications approved by the company and shall be subject to the joint supervision, inspection and acceptance of our chief engineer and the chief engineer of the commission. I beg to say if this work is done in accordance with what I understand to be your recent instructions, it will not be in compliance with the agreement nor satisfactory to this company and cannot be accepted.
This is something very forcible. What is Mr. Leonard's reason for making these changes ? (Reading):
I find on going over the profiles that there are many places where a large expenditure may be saved and the line actually improved for operating purposes, and the time of completion considerably shortened, without in the least affecting the hauling capacity of locomotives, by making certain modifications, and I have given instructions to make such modifications accordingly.
Here is the admission of Major Leonard that he has given instructions to have these profiles changed from what had been accepted by the Government and by the Grand Trunk engineers. Therefore, Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
there comes this reply from Mr. Chamberlin, the president of the company:
I have yours of the 19th instant regarding changes in grade on the National Transcontinental railway, and note the Teasons you offer for the modifications contemplated. Aside altogether from this company's strict rights, to which I called attention in my letter of the 18th instant to you, I would ask you to furnish me with profiles showing the changes proposed so that I may consider their effect. You will, I think, agree that it would be in the interests of both the commissioners and this company that no work in connection with any changes of grade should be proceeded with until our approval has been given, and I would ask you to issue instructions to this effect.
This is a most reasonable request. Mr. Chamberlin says to Major Leonard: I would like to have the profiles submitted to me. So far as I can understand the correspondence, this very legitimate request of Mr. Chamberlin was not complied with, because this is the reply of Major Leonard under date of August 2, 1912:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 23rd ultimo, expressing your apprehensions regarding the modifications referred to in my letter of the 19th ultimo.
I note you refer to your company's ' strict rights,' to whicih yon also referred in yours of the 18th, for which reference I can find no authority in the various Acts and agreements relating to the construction of the eastern division.
I must say that my astonishment could not be expressed when I heard that statement of Major Leonard, in which he coolly tells Mr. Chamberlin that, when he speaks of his ' strict rights ' under the contract, he does not understand what Mr. Chamberlin means. Is that the way that Major Leonard understands his duties ? Will my hon. friend assume the responsibility of telling this House that the Grand Trunk railway have mo rights under that contract ? Mr. Chamberlin referred Major Leonard to the very clause of the agreement, clause 7, which is in these terms:
In order to insure, foT the protection of the company as lessees of the eastern division of the said railway, the economical construction thereof in such a manner that it can be operated to the best advantage, it is hereby agreed that the specifications for the construction of the eastern division shall he submitted to and approved by the company before the commencement of the work, and that the said work shall he done according to the said specifications and shall be subject to the joint supervision, inspection and acceptance of the chief engineer appointed by the Government and the chief engineer of the company, and in the event of differences as to the specifications, or in case the said engineers shall differ as to the work, the questions in dispute shall be determined by the said engineers and a third arbitrator, to be chosen in the manner provided in paragraph four of this agreement.

That is the letter of the law. When Mr. Chamberlin refers Major Leonard to clause 7 of the contract, and insists upon that as defining his strict rights, he is told by Major Leonard that the latter does not understand what Mr. Chamberlin means. This manner of doing business is certainly very strange, and cannot pass muster in this Parliament. The letter of the law must be respected, quite apart from the merits of the case. When Major Leonard tells Mr. Chamberlin that he has no right, he is trifling with his position and is taking upon himself responsibilities which are not warranted and for which he has no mandate.
That is upon the formal, legal part of the question; now, come to the engineering part. You have seen that Major Leonard says in his first letter that the information given to Mr. Chamberlin is right, that he has given definite instructions to have changes made which he says will be for the bettering of the road. Let me Tead his letter again:	v
I find on going over the profiles, that there are many places where a large expenditure may be saved and the line actually improved for operating purposes, and the time of completion considerably shortened without in the least affecting the hauling capacity of locomotives, by making certain modifications, and I have given instructions to make such modifications accordingly.
Upon this, Mr. Chamberlin asked that he should be given the profiles of the proposed improvements. Does Major Leonard comply wit-h the request? That would be the reasonable, the fair, the businesslike thing to do. But, extraordinary as it appears, Major Leonard says that he has changed the plans, yet, when he is asked for new profiles, he will not comply with the request. This seems incredible, yet it is true. Then he goes on:
You have apparently been misinformed in regard to the reported changes in grade, as no change whatever in any of the ruling grades has been contemplated, but merely such trifles as slight local sags in the grades across soft swamps which will not in any way affect the hauling capacity of locomotives and which, if found desirable to lift out in the future for any unforseen reason, can be effected more cheaply than at present contract prices, and will make a more solid roadbed than is being made under similar circumstances to-day by using the peat for embankments.
What dods this change mean? At first, it was a matter of great consequence; Mr. Leonard says it is for the sake of economy and the improvement of the road. But when Mr. Chamberlin asks for the new profiles, he tells him, in effect: You need not worry, it is a matter of little consequence. Well, is it important or is it not important? Why have we not the
facts? Why all this mystery? There is something here very mysterious indeed, iand not in the best sense of the word. There is no possible justification for the attitude of the Government upon this question. My hon. friend is asking for a very large estimate, and we are prepared to vote it; but we want to know what these changes are, and whether the first letter of Mr. Leonard is right or is not right; whether the changes are of consequence or not of consequence. Why have we not this information? Does my hon. friend believe that he is right in asking us to vote this sum of money without giving us full information?
But that is not all. There are important legal questions involved which may develop serious consequences to the Government. Mr. Chamberlin said-and in saying it he was within his rights:
I beg to say that if this work is done in accordance with what I understand to be your recent instructions, it will not be in compliance with the agreement nor satisfactory to this company, and cannot be accepted.
I say Mr. Chamberlin is within his rights when he says he will not accept this work; in case of dispute, the only way by which a decision can be reached is by arbitration. I note that in the answer given by the Minister of Railways to my hon. friend from Carleton yesterday, the statement is made that the Grand Trunk Railway Company will accept the road. What reason has the minister for saying so? The hon. gentleman says again that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is the contractor for a part of the road, and he implies that they would have to accept the work done by themselves. That is not an answer. The Grand Trunk railway have lodged a protest in this matter; that is the only thing they could do-do the work as directed by the engineer in charge, and then lodge their protest. It would be no answer to the Grand Trunk railway, if they were to refuse to take over the road, to say that they were the contractors of the road, and that they themselves put in the momentum grades. Their answer would be: We protested^ but the work was gone on with. There is the position in which we are at the present time, and, I repeat, the position is not satisfactory, and we require more information on this question.
Then, as to the wooden structures. I do not quite understand the position. Yesterday, as I understand, it was stated that there were wooden structures. Mr. Chamberlin says so. But I understood my hon. friend the minister to say to-day that there are no wooden structures.

Temporary ones, but
all replaced by the others; and under the old commission it was done in the same way.

That is
assuming what is in issue. There is the statement of my hon. friend, and, on the other side, the statement of Mr. Chamberlin. Why is the matter not cleared up?
It is cleared up.
It is not sufficient merely to have the complaints on the one side and the answer on the other.
There was a contract given last week for eight or ten steel bridges to replace these temporary structures, and they are going in right along.

Possibly.
But we have to extract that information from my hon. friend; we have to extract it from him -almost bodily. Why does he not give us the information?
I said there was no change in the policy of construction.

But the
correspondence would show that there is.
I submit, with all due respect, that my hon. friend has not treated the committee properly. He should have given information as to these changes to show exactly what they are, what they are to cost -and how they will affect the character of the road.

I might point out to my right hon. friend the latter part of the letter sent by Mr. Leonard to Mr. Chamberlin :
I suggested in my letter of the 19th ultimo that your chief engineer or assistant chief engineer discuss with our chief engineer any proposed changes, and report to you in regard the same, because, you will see from the above, these are simply details too trifling to occupy either your attention or mine, and the suggestion in my letter of the 19th ultimo should be quite sufficient for your purposes.
Perhaps it would be still simpler and quite as efficient for you to get your information through your district engineers after consultation with the district engineers of the commission, in the usual way.
There is no reason to assume that Mr. Chamberlin did not get such information in the way he suggested. There is no reason to assume that he was not satisfied with it, because there is no reply from Mr. Chamberlin finding fault with the suggestion made by Mr. Leonard. It seems to me that it is a question between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as to the propriety of the Government's action in respect to the change of the grades, and scarcely a matter that ought to be discussed at this time between the parties in this House. The right is a right as between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, unless hon. | Mr. COCHRANE.
gentlemen opposite are holding a brief for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, which I do not suppose.

So Tar as I am concerned, I hold no brief for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company or for anybody else on earth. I am only stating my honest opinions, and I do not appreciate the intimation the hon. gentleman has made.
Did the hon. gentleman have his ear open to what I said? I said unless hon. gentlemen opposite were holding a brief for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, which I do not suppose.
That is a very unpleasant way of putting it.

I quite understand the assumed sensitiveness of the hon. member for Carleton. He started out last night, in reply to the hon. Minister of Railways, by stating that the statement of the hon. Minister of Railways in reply to the hon. member for South Renfrew, was an apology. If an apology is a statement of the truth, if an apology is the giving of good reasons for the action of the Government in changing the grades; if an apology means a plain statement of honest facts honestly made, then the statement of the hon. minister was an apology. The hon. member for Carleton does not appear to accept such an apology, because he is not willing-and I can understand it-to accept a plain statement of the truth in plain language, honestly made, and giving good reasons for the change.
Who gave them?

The hon. Minister of Railways gave them in his speech. Again the hon. member for Carleton sneers at the Government because they made savings. I am not at all surprised that the hon. member should do that; he apparently despises savings. The cause of that contempt for saving appears to be this. Durr ing the time the late Government had charge of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, it was quite evident to the country that they were reckless in expenditure, and did not care about economy in the construction of that railway; therefore the hon. gentleman despises saving. The hon. member for Carleton says that certain contractors should have received $18,000, and it was cheese-paring to prevent them from receiving it. If the contractors were entitled to that amount they had a course open to recover it, and that is the usual course.

If my hon. . friend
would read the contract, he would realize that what he has said just now has no

foundation in fact. Under the contract the contractor is bound to take the amount given him by the chief engineer, and he has no appeal or no rights in court.
Mr. AIKINS! The hon. gentleman knows that notwithstanding the fact that clauses are inserted in contracts, the courts still have a jurisdiction to decide what is right and what is proper.
I do not know any such thing.
I would advise the hon. gentleman to commence the study of law.
How could the contractor get into the Exchequer Court under such circumstances?

By commencing a suit, and if it be against the Crown and required they can do it by getting a fiat. The minister has told hon. gentlemen opposite that none of these contractors have appealed to him in respect of that. Why? Because their consciences told them that what had been done was right. Let me say a word in regard to the other point to which the right hon. gentleman referred, viz.: that the Government had no right to change the grades without knowing the benefit that would be derived therefrom, and the saving that would be effected. It must be obvious to any person who has any knowledge of railroading that a reduction of the amount that is placed in embankment or taken out of excavation must necessarily cause a saving, and when there is a four-tenths or six-tenths grade, which would be the top or surface of the grade, and a profile showing the natural condition of the earth, one can see at once that where a momentum grade is constructed between the two and where it is not brought up to the four-tenths or six-tenths grade, there must be a saving, which is the difference of cost between the virtual or momentum grade and the four-tenths or six-tenths grade. The point of the hon. gentleman is that the country should know exactly the amount of the saving. The amount was given in respect of two cases, about $27,000 I think, but when it comes to an approximate estimate of the saving over two hundred miles, that is a matter of calculation, not of the work done, but of the work omitted; a subtraction between what the four-tenths work would cost if it were done and what the grade actually did cost, in each particular instance. That would not be in the engineer's return. The Minister of Railways is perfectly right in saying that the Government is asking a man to make these calculations and that they will be immediately submitted to the House. It seems to n*e that the course of the Government in. the changing of the grade is perfectly reasonable because there is not a railway constructed in Canada-and the Canadian Pacific railway is a well constructed railway, as are other lines in Canada- that has not virtual or momentum grades, and the reason of that has been that it is in the interests of economy and good railway construction that there should be such grades. It is almost axcomatic that where the railway is thus constructed and it becomes necessary to raise the grade in order to make it a four-tenths or six-tenths grade, it is quite easy to do it after the rails are laid. Therefore, I submit that the action of the Government was right.

It is well-known that
momentum1 grades were introduced by the Canadian Pacific railway to get rid of grades that had no momentum. As this-road was intended to be level, I presume the principle to which my hon. friend adheres is that momentum grades are introduced to make it easier to carry a load than it would be to carry it on a level, track. The hon. member asserts that Parliament should have nothing to do with these grades; that that is a question between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Government. I think my hon. friend will readily see the fallacy of that argument. This road belongs to the people of Canada, and not to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. It is being leased to them, but it is our property.	We made a	contract
with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and an agreement was entered into that the road should conform to a certain standard. We told the people of Canada that we would build to that standard. It is a violation of the agreement between this Parliament and the people of Canada, and it is our business to look after the construction of our own roads.
The hon. gentleman hasreferred to an agreement made. Who were the parties to the agreement?

The agreement made
between the Government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Pacific in the statute, and an agreement made, a promise absolutely made to the people of Canada, in 1908, that the road would be built to a standard described as four-tenths of one per cent against eastbound and six-tenths of one per cent against westbound traffic.

Will you tell me
who authorized the change from five-tenths-to six-tenths going west?

The change was made
on the recommendation of the chief engineer, accepted by the commission and approved by the Grand Trunk Pacific.
There is no record of it.

It is the case. It has
been proved all the way through, and their road west of Winnipeg is built on the same standard, which is good proof.
Were the people consulted about that?

That was in 1904, and
the change was made in 1907; these standards were submitted to the people in the election of 1908 on every platform of Canada, and the election of 1908 was fought on the Grand Trunk Pacific. Hon. gentlemen opposite or their friends had all their literature aimed at the great cost that this railway was to be to the people of Canada. We admitted the cost but said that the people would have the benefit. Why? The road would be of a higher standard than any competing road on the continent, and the people of Canada would have the benefit. The Government was returned overwhelmingly on that standard, and I say that constituted a promise by the Government of Canada to the people of Canada that has been violated by this Government. It is our business in Parliament, because it is our road, our undertaking, under the agreement. The hon. member says that this is an agreement between the Government and the Grand Trunk and that it is none of our business. I say it is wrong, because this road, constructed by this Parliament, is our road and is to remain the road of the people of Canada.

The engineer says
there was 300,000 yards of earth at thirty cents and 150,000 yards of rock at $1,101.

That only shows the
value that you can place on the statement of the hon. member for St. Antoine. He goes down there with his little pick and shovel and comes back and tells Parliament things that are not true, and unless there was someone here who knew something about it the statements would go out as the truth. He told-you that there were
400,000	yards of material put in there at $1,101 when it should have been bridged Mr. COCHRANE. *
with steel and concrete. He did not say what the difference would be, but the inference was that it would cost less to have a steel viaduct than a solid fill. I am not engineer enough to argue the difference, but it does not require an engineer to know that you would have a better road with solid filling than with a steel viaduct, because sometime the steel viaduct will wear out or break or require repairing. When you have a solid fill it is there forever, and as the hon. member for South Eenfrew (Mr. Graham) pointed out, this is not the Grand Trunk's railway, we are not giving away millions of dollars, as my hon. friend proposes to do this week to Mackenzie and Mann, but we are building a road for ourselves; it is our property, and every dollar that we put in it is our property, and it comes back to us in forty years, so that the more we put into it now, the more valuable we make it, the better our property will be then, and the better it will be for the country and for the company operating it. Therefore, I say that the Government was justified in filling the holes with such material if they could get it done cheaply, and it is a much better road than any steel viaduct would be. If my hon. friend could see this particular place to which reference is made, he would understand it. You approach the place by a curve, you have a very long deep fill, something that would require a .great deal of care if a steel viaduct were placed there, and with a solid fill it is there for all time. I have heard the matter discussed a good many times, and my recollection is that it figured somewhere about sixty cents a yard, less than sixty cents as the cost of filling that enormous fill. That would compare favourably with the cost of a viaduct, the cost is about the same, or in other words you have got your hole filled with solid material for about the same money as the steel would have cost, and you have a much better road.
The hon. member spoke of the work to be found on contract No. 5, in which he said a large amount of material had been used as fill, costing $1,101 per yard. That is true; I will give him credit for telling the truth there; but if the hon. member for St. Antoine had wanted to be fair to the committee and to give the facts to the House, he would have gone back three or four years to a return brought down in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for York, N.B. (Mr. Crocket) which told the whole story. It showed what it would cost to build it with steel and concrete. That , is the cost of a viaduct would be so many hunderd thousand dollars. _ The only material which could be obtained, within four or five miles of that particular location, was rock, and they figured out what the cost of a viaduct would be and estimated the price per yard for rock filling that would

bring the same total. The chief engineer found that the contractor would have to put in the material at $1.10i in order to bring the total -down to the cost of steel. I hope it will do good to my hon. friend! from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames). This is no secret information that I am giving to the public. Every hon. member of this House could get it just as well as I could if he applied for it. I am not giving away any secrets, and my hon. friend from St. Antoine can get the information just as well as I can, and so can my hon. friend enough about railway matters to understand enough about railway matters to understand these things when he reads them. I do not refer to the chief engineer. The chief engineer is all right. It is the man my hon. friend has been sending round over the head of the chief engineer to whom I refer. Does my hon. friend want the name?
Yes.

He also stated that the gradients had been changed so as to give less work. In so doing the work has been lessened a great deal and by that means so much money is being saved for the public treasury. I do not deny that this is a drawback as far as the train circulation is concerned, because an engine cannot draw as many cars up a gradient as it would on a level road or where the gradient are small, but it is false to say that in the work of construction the country is losing hundreds of thousands of dollars which go to swell the contractor's profit.
It is well that the facts should be stated as they are so as to prevent the hon member for Montcalm from going round in his county saying, I have stated such and such facts on the floor of the House and not one of the Conservative members has denied them. Not only in the province of Quebec have changes been made on the Transcontinental railway. The hon. Postmaster

General has promptly corrected the hon. member for Montcalm, stating the real facts and telling him that such changes have been made on the whole length of the line which remains to be 'built. That is the real truth and what was said by the hon. member for Montcalm is untrue. These changes affect the portions of that railway running through New Brunswick and -Ontario as well as in Quebec wherever the road is still unfinished. Therefore, the changes are not attributable to a feeling of antipathy towards the province of Quebec, but are for the benefit of the public. That is another of the falsehoods which it was important to deny, for the Government have not acted through [DOT]antipathy towards the province of Quebec, as stated by the hon. member for Montcalm.
It is very easy to make charges right and left without giving any proof. Has not Voltaire said: 'Tell lies repeatedly and something thereof will always remain.' I do not know whether the hon. member has read Voltaire or not, but judging from what he said this afternoon, he seems to have studied that author.
He also spoke about the increase of expenses. He said that the public expenses have largely increased since the Conservatives are in power and he claims it is a thing unheard of. The hon. member for Montcalm has had the honour of having for a number of years held a seat in the former Parliament. Now he ought to know that it is not only under Conservative rule that the expenses have increased. In 1876, when the Conservatives were in power the expenses were only 40 ox 42 millions, and when the ex-Premier, now leader of the Opposition, left power in 1911, the public expenses had reached 136 millions. And the hon. member is really shocked to-day at the fact that the expenses have increased by a few millions, and still it must be said that this increase is, to a large extent, due to the work being done on the Transcontinental and for which several millions appear in the estimates. Quebec bridge, $3,000,000.
How is the work progressing, on that bridge ?

In 1912 the south main caisson was sunk and filled with concrete, the work being completed on the 25th October. During the same season the foundation for the south anchor pier was made and twenty feet of concrete put in place. The total amount of masonry to be laid is 105,000 cubic yards, and the amount laid to the close of last season was 63,792 cubic yards. There remains to be laid 41,208 cubic yards, so that about two-thirds have been completed. The north abutment is finished. The north outer pier is finished; south main pier, about fifty per cent done; north main pier, seventy-five per cent done; north anchor pier, fifty per cent done; south anchor pier, ten per cent done. I expect that the contract will be fully completed this year. About one hundred men are employed now.
Do I understand that it is expected that the masonry work will be completed this year ?
Yes, the contract was to be finished last year, but we extended it.
When will the superstructure be completed ?

I will give the data which was given to me by the chairman of the board of engineers that has the work in charge. The contractors have during the past year completed a new plant at Roekfield, Quebec, and they have turned out a large quantity of material. This new plant has been in operation since the first of this year and about one Mr. COCHRANE.
thousand five hundred tons of the members of the bridge have been fabricated, and part of the material has been sent to the bridge site. Steel for the false work, crane, &o., is being shipped to the site. Ten thousand tons of steel has been ordered from the mills at Pittsburg, and of this, six thousand two hundred tons have been delivered at the shops at Roekfield and two thousand tons of the same have been manufactured. The contractors are putting in the concrete foundations for the false work, for the approach span and for the crane runways on the north side, and are erecting false work on the south -side. The steel for the anchorage has been completed. The crane runway in the unloading yards are about ready for operation. Regular shipments of steel to the site will be commenced shortly. Mr. Montserrat and

completed, would be entitled to some honour in this country if he made a success of it. I was very ambitious that such an honour should come to a Canadian. I am glad Mr. Montserrat is making good in fulfilling our expectations.

There will be eventually.
I see now why my hon. friend from East Simeoe (Mr. Bennett) is so keenly in favour of this.

I would advise hon. gentlemen on the other side to take a trip over this Trent Valley water system. When it is opened into Georgian bay, as it will be under the present Administration, there will be a capacity in the large elevators at Port McNichol and Midland of nearly
10,000,000 bushels. It is contended that as the old Erie canal succeeded in carrying grain in barges with a capacity of only
7.000	bushels, with barges on this canal carrying over 15,000 bushels, a large trade can be done from Port McNichol to Montreal. If the grain is not carried by such barges to Montreal, the canal will at least have the effect of keeping down the rates on the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway from these two points. I understand that the minister's policy is to make the canal eight feet over the locks on all the new work. The old work is six feet, but that can be deepened at a comparatively low cost. If you had a waterway through lake Simeoe and through the large lakes and rivers in that district, you could have barges carrying
20.000	bushels of grain. You would be in a position that the grain trade of lake Ontario was in twenty years ago. I can recall when the American grain which came from Chicago and Fort William for transit to the Old Country, and for distribution

in Canada and the United States, was carried in schooners containing only about
20,000	bushels. We will have there a waterway with an eight-foot depth and barges that will carry 20,000 bushels of grain. It is to be regretted that the general public take no cognizance of the extent and capacity of these waterways. Take lake Simcoe, which is from fifteen to twenty miles wide, and the lakes below Peterborough, a number of which are quite large lakes. It is true there are points where there are canal connections, but there you have a series of large lakes. Historically speaking, I may point out that Governor Simcoe had a survey made of this area comprising these waterways over one hundred years ago. With prophetic vision he saw what is happening to-day and what is likely to happen in the near futnre when this series of waterways will be connected with lake Ontario and Georgian bay.

I may point out that
long before Simcoe, Champlain went up the Trent valley and predicted that one day the great lakes would be connected. That is why the Government are erecting a statue to Champlain at Orillia.

I do not believe that large quantities of grain will be carried over that system, because transportation will be slower than by rail, but I think it will have the effect of bringing the railway companies to time, and that it will force them to give better rates than exist at the present time. I have no apology to offer for the Trent canal system as a tourist route. If, when it is finished, it becomes the greatest tourist system on the continent, it will be well worth the money spent upon it. We all know the Muskoka lakes. The Grand Trunk will tell you that every' year there pass over the docks at Gravenhurst over 50,000 tourists. Think of what that means for this country! Once completed through to the Georgian bay the canal will provide a waterway for gasoline yachts and, the locks being 130 feet in length, a person will be able to leave New York city in a yacht 130 feet long, drawing not more than six feet of water, because a great many of these yachts are gasoline craft, come up to lake Champlain, go into the St. Lawrence at Sorel, pass by the Trent, clear through to the Georgian bay and on to the Sault, returning by way of the St. Clair and Detroit rivers and the Welland canal. I think that in fairness to the Trent Valley canal every member of this House should take a trip to Peterborough and on up from there. He will not only be impressed by the beauty of the route, but he will realize the wonderful opportunities there are for
building up an enormous tourist trade. Americans have gone to these lakes back of Peterborough and have built residences costing $7,000 or $8,000. It is going to be a great tourist country, and if we can, by completing this work, attract from New York and all over the world, hundreds and thousands of tourists, the country will be well repaid for the effort and the outlay.

I think the minister ought to give us a little more information about the total cost of this canal. We have embarked upon very large expenditures in connection with these canals, and the people would like to know what this canal is going to cost when completed. The minister appears to adopt a different principle in canals to that which he lays down with reference to railways. When a branch railway is asked for in the province of Nova Scotia he lays down the doctrine that you must not only show that there is traffic enough to give us interest on our money, but-
Do not give me credit for this work. I did not start it; it was started in 1880.

I am not objecting to
the canal being started, but I want to know what the total cost is to be when completed. I am not opposing the construction of the canal. I do not know very much about it. I know that lake Simcoe is a very beautiful sheet of water and I quite agree with what the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) says that a tourist traffic might be developed there. I am not saying that the canal will not be useful for tourist traffic and other purposes, but I wish to draw attention to the fact that the minister regards expenditure on canals in a different way from that in which he seems to regard expenditure on the Intercolonial railway. I do not know why he should. I hope it is not because the canal happens to be situated in the province of Ontario. As a matter of fact we do not expect any revenue at all from the canals. We are building them at a very large expense to the country. The traffic, I understand, pays nothing. That may be all right, but I think that the minister ought to take a different view in regard to the question of railways just as he does with regard to the question of canals. I agree with him that he ought to assist traffic through our country and I am not opposing this policy. What I rose for was to press the minister to give us some idea of what the cost of this canal will be when completed.
I am told about $16,000,000.

We have heard
so much about the canal, historically and geographically, that I feel justified in try-

mg to learn a little more about it. It is quite an ancient work because we find there was a survey made by the late Governor Simcoe, and my hon friend from Eouville (Mr. Lemieux) has told us that Champlain indicated in a prophetical way that some day we would cross that part of Canada through a canal. From the hon. member for York we ascertained that it was a creek and that finally it turned out to be quite an ocean, 21 miles wide at certain places. Now it turns out to be a series of lakes. It seems to me that this canal has become an -eternal question. We have just learned from the Minister of Railways and Canals that it is a series of canals connecting a series of lakes and that it will cost the people $11,000,000. The hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. White) is taking just as great an interest in the Georgian Bay canal as I am myself and we see that this Trent Valley canal has swallowed up about $11,000,000 of our money with no practical results. We want to know if there is any part of this work, begun in 1880, which is being utilized in some way, either to produce power or electricity or for the purpose of small navigation or the navigation of large tonnage. I cannot understand how it is that after we have spent $11,000,000 and after this work has been under construction for the last thirty-three years we have not achieved any practical result exceipt that we are able to say that a nice yacht 130 feet long with a draught of 6 feet and propelled by gasolene or electricity may pass through it. Has the late Conservative Administration before 1896 been idle, has the late Liberal Government been idle?

Yes, both idle, and we
are trying to get them going.

The hon. member for
Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) says that the construction of this canal is so difficult, that there are so many geographical and natural obstacles, that from 1880 to 1897 his friends who were then in power, were not able to overcome them?
The difficulties are not physical but political.
And these difficulties have existed for the last thirty-three years?
Yes, all over Canada.
Well, that is something strange.
It is very odd.

I would like to know from the minister what he proposes to do with the million dollars which he mentioned a few minutes ago. Is that included in the $11,000,000 which have already been spent?
Mr. WILSON (Laval).

No, the $11,000,000
was the expenditure up to March 31, 1912. I may -say that we need this million dollars to complete work that has -been under contract for a number of years.

$16,000,000 altogether.
And it is expected that the work will be completed by 1915 or 1916?
In two years, I hope.

If you are still in power, I suppose this House and the country will have to give you credit if you succeed in completing the work. In order that each administration should take the responsibility for what has or has not been done, or has been done in a wrong way, I would like to know how much has been spent from 1880 to 1897, what amount of work has been done, what has been done by the Liberal Administration, what the hon. minister proposes to do, and what is the balance of the work to be done.

This amount will
complete the work to lake Ontario. Unfortunately, whatever administration started the work, they started it in the middle, instead of starting it either at -one outlet or the other.

The reverse of the

I -shall be glad to get the information required.

Has the Postmaster
General any plans in view with regard to increasing the salaries of country postmasters?

knowledge, but if I can trust our post office inspector there, the people are wrong in supposing that this young lady has been made a scapegoat of. According to the files, the facts are absolutely as I have stated them to my hon. friend.

It strikes me that the
position of my hon. friend the Postmaster General is absolutely untenable. He removed a postmaster who gave every satisfaction, absolutely without cause except the charge of being a partisan. He appointed another gentleman as postmaster, who was admittedly a partisan, who was appointed because he was a partisan, and who not only was a partisan but was a leader of my hon. friend's partisans in that particular locality. After he was appointed, instead of there being efficiency of administration, there was such inefficiency that it came to the attention of the department. There was the appearance of dishonesty. It is most remarkable that an efficient man is removed; that the office is administered inefficiently, to the scandal of the neighbourhood, and that my hon. friend not only does not remove the postmaster, but does not censure him. He tells us that he has removed the postmaster's niece. He brings before the attention of the House and of the country the suggestion that this young woman, this assistant of the postmaster, is the person who is responsible, although he has not a tittle of evidence to bring before the House to that effect. such a way. Does my hon. friend think the post office service of this_ country is only for the purpose of providing recognition for political partisans? and I think, as long as the present postmaster remains in office, the people of Gran'by will be satisfied. In the month of November, 1912, certain petitions were sent to the department of the Postmaster General, and also to the right hon. the Premier from the letter carriers' union at Sydney, and from the federated association of letter carriers which represents ninety-eight per cent of the letter carriers in the Dominion. They have submitted for the consideration of the

department certain changes which would be oi great benefit to them. They submitted that they were entitled to an eight-hour day; to sick pay, which I understand they are not getting at present; and also that they should have .a half holiday each week during the months of June, July and August, that is in the heat of the summer. They also submitted a very strong case for an increase in salary. With reference to the weight of mail, those resolutions set forth that at that time and I understand there has been no change since-the letter carriers are obliged to carry .between ninety and one hundred and fifteen pounds of mail. I do not think that men can do justice to themselves or to the delivery 6f mail if they are obliged to carry that weight. I understood some time ago tnat, under the regulations of the department, the weight of mail which they are obliged to carry is somewhat less than that. Therefore it must be the case that we have not got sufficient letter carriers in order to make the postmasters in the various cities see to it that they carry the regulation weight. These resolutions were submitted to me some time ago, also the question of superannuation and uniforms, as well as other questions. I think all these resolutions should commend themselves to the serious consideration of the Post Office Department. Officers who are obliged to be about in all kinds of weather as letter carriers are should not be obliged to work more than eight hours a day in view of the fact that they are working for a Government and a department that can well afford to see to it that they do not work longer. If an employee -in the inside service is sick for a day or two he is given his pay while off duty, but it seems that the letter carriers are only paid by the day and that if one of them is off a day through sickness, he is docked a day's pay. This seems discriminatory and unfair. Then there is the question of the half holiday. I do not know what attention the Postmaster General has given to these resolutions, but if he has not dealt with them, I think it only fair that he should do what is possible to remedy the grievances of the letter carriers. I do not think they are asking too much. They are a low-paid class of men; they have to work long hours, and they carry heavy loads. I understand that the letter carriers in the city of Sydney, who are all good men so far as I know, were represented in the delegation which came to the minister, and I have no doubt they made their complaints more strongly than I could, for it is only recently' that these resolutions were placed in my hands. I look to the minister to say whether these things have been taken into consideration and whether they have been remedied or will be remedied.

The representations of the letter carriers were laid before me last
fall or winter by the delegation of which the hon. gentleman speaks. The rule about the eight hour day is being enforced. Of course, as every hon. member will understand, it inevitably happens that trains are sometimes late, and in such cases the letter carriers must work more than eight hours. But the instructions from the department are that these cases shall be recognized by making an allowance, or giving the men more rest on the following day, or something of that kind. But the rule is for eight hours work a day and the officers of the department are carrying out that rule. As to the weight the letter carriers must take, the department thinks it well to leave that to the judgment of the postmaster. Every postmaster knows that the desire of the department is that these men should not 'be overburdened, and that if they are not numerous enough to take care of the whole delivery in one trip, some of the stuff should remain in the office for further delivery. Oi course, the letters will be taken care of in/ any _ case by the first delivery, but parcels and newspapers may have to wait when they are in too great quantity. Now, as to sick nay, these men already receive sick pay where the department has been notified that the sickness is a bona fide one. I remember telling our friends, the letter carriers, when their representatives came here, that they were entitled to sick pay. They said that this rule was ignored; I told them that if the rule was not carried out they might make their representations in the regular way and their complaint would be attended to. This covers three points raised by my hon. friend. The fourth is the question of the half-holiday. I have, as he will see, gone into these matters pretty carefully. The half-holiday question is the one not settled so far. I have referred it to the officers of the department for a report, and I understand that that report will be placed before me as soon as the arduous, work of the session is over. I agree that the work of the letter carriers is important and that they should be well treated. We have a good staff of letter carriers and I have much sympathy with them. And I think they will find that I have something more than mere cold sympathy.

And I hope the Postmaster General will have something more than cold sympathy for the rural postmasters. My hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) has spoken on their behalf, and I endorse everything he has said. I think that their salary should be increased, and that the minimum should be $50 year.

The Postmaster General
has said we have to be dissatisfied in order to get information. I am going to ask him

a question about something with which I am not satisfied. I desire to know the reason for the dismissal of Mr. J. Masse, postmaster at Roxton Falls.
He was dismissed for political partisanship.
Would the minister please *look over the file and, the next time the committee meets and takes up the Post Office estimates, give me some details concerning the nature of that political partisanship?
I will.

I hope the Postmaster
General will not have too strong a grudge against me if I refer to the changes in the officers of his department in my riding. I allowed the whole of last session to pass without making any reference to the matter. I have here the latest edition of the Postal Guide in which I see that there are about eighty-three post offices in Bonaventure. I have not had any return since the 5th of March last as to the number disnyssed, but I think that roughly speaking there must have been thirty or thirty-five changes through dismissal. The dismissals were for alleged political partisanship.
During the last campaign I had the good fortune of having as my opponent Mr. Mousseau, a son of the late Prime Minister of Quebec, who afterwards undertook to communicate with the department with a view to giving to Caesar the things that are Caesar's or in other words, of urging that some of the spoils be given to Conservative supporters in his constituency. A dead set was made upon practically every office held in the constituency, and the principle upon which action was taken in this regard is laid down by Mr. Mousseau in a letter addressed to the Postmaster General dated November 9, 1911. It is in French, but I have translated it as follows:
Hon. L. P. Pelletier,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa.
Sir,-I have received several communications from your department on the subject of the appointment of Mr. Franpois Dion as postmaster at Caplan River. I will draw your attention to this subject by my letter of October 21 last addressed to the deputy minister. It is needless for me to say that applications are numerous since the elections. Since the elections we have been very busy and I have not been able to deal with all requests that have been made. and it is better to take our time and act so as to please our friends.

This indicates exactly the line of action under which proceedings were taken at that time. In Shigawake, one of the Englishspeaking centres of the county, Mr. James Poirier, postmaster, who had been dismissed in 1896, was reinstated on the request of Mr. Mousseau, and against the protests of practically the entire population. Mr. J. A. LeGallais, the postmaster and storekeeper of the place, a man who gave eminent satisfaction, not only to the department but to the public as well, was dismissed and replaced by Mr. James Poirier, who held office up to 1896. It was alleged that Mr. Poirier had been dismissed for political reasons, but he was really dismissed for other reasons. Here is a letter written by Mr. Mousseau to the Postmaster General on March 2, 1912:
I have tlie honour to ask that (Mr. James Poirier, of Shigawake, he appointed postmaster at that place in the place of John LeGallais, the present postmaster. In support of this request I submit that Mr. LeGallais is a political partisan, and has been, even Since the elections, and that Mr. James Poirier is one of our most faithful friends in the county. Mr. Poirier should he reinstated without inquiry, as he was dismissed from his functions for political reasons in 1896.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant, < J. A. Mousseau.
