I am in receipt of your letter of the 15th instant, stating that you understand there is a question of a change in the site and postmastership of Shigawake, Que., and expressing satisfaction with the present site and management of that office, and, in reply, beg to state that your representations in the matter will receive careful consideration.
Several letters seem to have been addressed to the Postmaster General by Mr. Mousseau and other Conservatives in the district asking that Mr. LeGallais be dismissed, and that Mr. Poirier be reinstated. This seems to have been done, notwithstanding the protest of the reverend gentleman whom I have mentioned. I will read the protest addressed by him to the Prime Minister:
Saint Paul's Episcopal Parsonage,
Shigawake, Bonaventure county, P.Q., March 3, 1913.
To the Right Hon. R. L. Borden,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Sir,-I have for some time now been *writing my Conservative friends to try and get the present post office in Shigawake moved to a more central place so that the demands of the public here might be satisfied, but as yet -the only satisfaction that I can get is a letter from the Post Office Department that the office has gone back to the holder of it in 1896, who lives remote from the centre, and who lost it in that year on this very account. I then went to Mr. Jos. Hayes and later to Mr. J. A. LeGallais, who kept the best post office that ever was in -Shigawake, and where the public got -the best of satisfaction, but, as, unfortunately, the post office seems to go with the spoils of war, Mr. LeGallais lost it.
and that not because be canvassed, but -because he was a Liberal. The result has been that ever since the public have suffered from, want of -proper shelter on account of the waiting-room having no -handle or lock, and, from cold for want of a stove, from fatigue from travelling too far for their mail, and from carelessness oh account of the postmaster frequently making all sorts of -mistakes. Recently I mailed a letter to Mrs. Jane Vi-bert and had same properly stamped and addressed to 816 Ames street, Saginaw, Mich., and the same night got- the same letter returned in my mail, without it having left the office. Again I am frequently given mail addressed to a Mr. Vautier here, and the other day Mr. Vautier mailed a letter to a Mr. Vautier in Boston, Mass., properly stamped and addressed, and the same *was given to me in -my mail without it having left the office. Again, till I corrected the post office people, they would not give me a money order for any sum less than $1, but wanted to issue postal notes, and the other day gave a postal note to our maid and made it payable in Jersey, Eng. On Sunday, 2nd, I supposed that I had obtained all my mail, but this a.m. got some that bad not been given me. This is of frequent occurrence. I know of several others who have complained about this same thing and earnestly hope that our present Government will comply with the manifest wishes of the people and place the office in the centre of -Shigawake.	-
Mr. J. A. LeGallais -was and is still a most respected merchant of the place. Mr. Jas. Poirier is a sewing machine agent and has to keep the office in the manner above stated as he has no store. I have a congregation of 409 souls here, the only clergyman living in the place, and the only one with a church in the -place, -the Roman Catholic -being at Stt Godfroy, and I think it only right, under these circumstances, that the voice of the people as expressed through my letters to the department, be given some attention, and the office returned to the centre and preferably to Mr. J. A. LeGallais, but if not to him,1 then I am -prepared to -recommend some other.
The Government will have all to gain and nought to lose by complying with this re-* quest.
Trusting I may be favoured with a favourable answer.
I have the honour to be,
Yours sincerely,
(Rev.) A. J. Vi-bert,
Church of England clergyman in charge of Shigawake and Hopetown.
These appeals were made in May. Mr. Le Gallais has given satisfaction, even Mr. Thos. Crockett, a former opponent of mine, appealed to the Postmaster General in favour of this recommendation, but to no effect. The Postmaster General followed the recommendation of Mr. Mousseau, who is acting with a view to helping the Conservative party, and the appointment of Mr. Poirier was made. His office is outside the village, and it has given great dissatisfaction. The result there is an evidence of the evil effects of making changes in post offices for political purposes. I have

not the patience nor would I be warranted in troubling the House with the numerous instances I have before me of dismissals of all kinds, but I would like to give one other dismissal, at St. Charles de Caplin, in spite of the protest of the parish priest and the great bulk of the people using the post office. In all of these dismissals the Postmaster General seems to have taken no account of the representations made by the clergy of the county.
These gentlemen are not partisans, and are speaking in the interest of the public I am sorry that the .Postmaster General followed the advice of Mr. Mousseau and gave the spoils to the friends of the party instead of following the advice of these gentlemen. Mr. Theophile Poirier, the postmaster, was dismissed in 1897. There was no evidence given. I have a personal recollection of having taken part in the election at that time. This man was dismissed for alleged political partisanship. When the Conservative Government came into power in September, 1911, an application was made by Mr. Robertson, of New Richmond, a strong Conservative, to reinstate Mr. Poirier. A letter was sent to Mr. Mousseau, and Mr. Mousseau agreed with the recommendation. The Postmaster General, ox one of his officials acting under him, gave instructions to [DOT] dismiss Mr. Arsenault and to appoint Mr. Poirier. The house of Poirier was no longer in the centre of the parish, it was quite a long distance from the church and at once there was a strong protest against that appointment, because it would put the whole parish to great inconvenience. A petition was sent to the Postmaster General, signed by the Reverend Mr. de Champlain and by practically all those using the office, protesting against the change. I shall not read the correspondence. The gist of it was that Arseneau had given good satisfaction, he had lately erected a post office building on the highway, and the office was situated close to the church. The removal of the office to Poirier's residence would not be at all satisfactory. The department, after a great deal of correspondence, decided to bring back the post office to the church and they appointed a new postmaster, Mr. L. Z. Leclaire. Leclaire's office was to be named St. Charles de Caplan, and Poirier's office should be given another name. The result was that Leclaire finally secured the name of St. Charles de- Caplan *and the other office was given the name of Mousseau. But there was already a post office of that name in Soulanges county and, therefore, this comedy of errors had to be re-enacted with the result that there is a second post office within a mile of that with the name of Mousseauville, and I do not suppose that Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure).
there is one person in the province of Quebec who would address any person living in St. Charles de Caplan as living at Mousseauville. The result is that the whole post office business has gone back to the church and the post office of Leclaire. Arsenault . who gave satisfaction has been dismissed and Mr. Mousseau has had his say. That is another instance of the unsatisfactory result of changes made for political purposes. In the parish of Avignon the postmaster was dismissed for the reinstatement of the former postmaster. The former postmaster was Octave Martin. Mr. Octave Martin was reinstated in October or November, 1912, but I understand that Octave Martin never attended to the post office at all, but that the post office was kept in the store of Blanquiere & Arsenault. The result is that lately I put a question >or two on the Order Paper and this probably attracted attention to the state of affairs, that Octave Martin, although postmaster, gave no attention to the post office which was in the store of another firm. The result was that Poirier, who had given great satisfaction to the whole parish, whose house is alongside the church, has been dismissed and a new postmaster has been appointed. In this instance I do not think that Mousseau's recommendation was taken into account 'because I understand that lately the patronage has passed into the hands of Mr. D. Champoux, of Campbellton, wbo was chosen at a meeting and who has come here on many occasions in connection with a local railway and with public works. I think this change was made on his recommendation.
In the parish of Bonaventure, the largest in the constituency, Charles Forest was dismissed and replaced by Firmin Poirier. Forest had been brought up in the post office. His father was postmaster at Bonaventure river for forty years and, this old man having retired, I had Charles Forest appointed at the request of Father Gravel parish priest, and with the practically unanimous support of the whole parish. I have here a petition -stating that Forest was the ideal postmaster of the locality. He has been brought up in the post office, as I said, he knew all the people, had given- eminent satisfaction to everybody.
He was dismissed simply because one night he met a fellow parishioner, and, talking about the elections, expressed the opinion that Mr. Marcil would he elected, or something to that effect. I am sorry to say that the dismissal has caused very general dissatisfaction even among Conservatives. At Caplin River there was an extraordinary state of affairs. Mr. Xavier Babin was dismissed and Mr. Denis Babin was appointed in his place. The ground of dismissal was alleged partisanship. Three recommendations were made by three former

opponents of my own, and a battle royal took place. Finally Mr. Mousseau gained the day. Mr. Babin was appointed because he had given more faithful service to the Conservative party than the two others. A protest has been sent by the Conservative electors, members of Le Comite de St. Charles de Caplan to the hon. Postmaster General against the appointment of Mr. Babin, and the result is that the change has caused general dissatisfaction in that locality, whereas the man who held the position before, gave complete satisfaction. I might mention one or two more cases. I understand that some of the appointments that were proposed have not been made. I would like to refer to St. Omer, one of the new parishes in the county. The postmaster in St. Omer, was Mr. Isidore Landry. After the hon. Postmaster General came into office, a communication was sent to him by the parish priest, the Rev. L. P. Chenard. It was signed by a number of people, and I would like to read it. I think their recommendation should have been followed. The letter was as follows:
To the Honourable L. P. Pelletier, Postmaster General,
Ottawa.
Honourable Sir,-The undersigned humbly set forth:
1.	That it is asked that the St. Omer post office be removed from the residence of Hr. Isidore Landry.
2.	That the said Isidore Landry has kept that post office for ten years.
3.	That no complaint has been laid, but on the contrary the public is well satisfied with the manner the office is kept and with the services of the postmaster.
4.	That the office is situated near the railway station and consequently centrally located.
5.	That your petitioners ask that the office shall not be removed.
6.	And that the said Isidore Landry be kept as postmaster as long as he gives satisfaction to everybody.
And your petitioners will ever pray.
Mr. Isidore Landry was dismissed to make room for Mr. Arseneau. The latter had been postmaster for a number of years up to the time he was appointed Crown lands agent for the province of Quebec. The department contended that it-was not in the public interest that a postmaster should hold a federal and a provincial position at the same time, and Mr. Arseneau was asked to resign, and he was removed from office on that ground. Subsequently, having been removed frcm the provincial office, he naturally applied to get back his post office, and the post office has been given to him not because of any particular complaint against Mr. Landry, "but because Mr. Arseneau had been the Conservative candidate in the county, had been a former postmaster, and was recommended by his political friends. I have not a word to say against Mr. Arseneau. He is a respectable
man, a man of high standing in the community, but he is pretty well up in years, and I know that if the Postmaster General's inspectors inquired as to how this post office was being conducted now, and as to how it was conducted by Mr. Landry, they would find it was more satisfactory under the old system than at present. There are any number of other cases. Apparently no one escaped. Wherever it was possible to make a dismissal, it was made, and whenever the appointment of a Conservative could be made it was made, and entirely for political services. There is the case of Robitaille in the same constituency. The post office there was formerly occupied by Mr. Edouard Quinn, a very respectable old gentleman, who gave satisfaction to the department and to the locality. A letter enclosing a blank form was sent to him, stating that certain charges had been made against him, and asking him to fill up the form and to make an affidavit that he had taken no part in the election. He made a statement before a justice of the peace, but Mr. Dagneau, a most active partizan, was appointed postmaster in his place. Since his appointment Mr. Dagneau has continued to look after the distribution of the patronage throughout the constituency. It was stated to me in a letter that the postmaster was really Mr. Joseph Dagneau, a brother of the man said to have been appointed. Mr. Quinn was a very deserving postmaster who gave complete satisfaction to the department and to the locality. He asked for an investigation, but it was refused. I do not think it is necessary for me to go into the other cases. I will merely name some of the places where charges have been, made. At Gravel Mr. F. J. Bujold was dismissed for alleged partisanship and Mr. Vincent Bujold was appointed. At Little Cascape-dia John B. Cyr was dismissed for alleged political partisanship, and Felix Arsenault was appointed. At Petit Bonaventure Joseph Belanger was dismissed for alleged political partisanship, and John Gallagher was appointed; at St. Godfrey, Laurent Huard was dismissed; and at New Richmond Centre a change was also made and the department gave the appointment to the old postmaster. I shall not say any more than merely express the regret that I feel that the Postmaster General, in making these various changes, seems to have followed the old political methods. I am sorry that the Postmaster General did not consider the interests of the service rather than the political interests of his party. I think the Postmaster General -will do well in future, whenever it is possible, to consider the public interest-the interest of the majority of the people who are served by the post office-Tather than the political interests of his party, and that he should also give consideration to

the question whether the postmaster ;has performed his duties satisfactorily or not. A warning might be appropriate to any person who has been found to have participated in politics, but who has given good service, such as Mr. Forest, of Bonaventure, because you have the evidence of the parish priest and the great hulk of the people interested declaring that he was the most competent man who had ever kept this office. Yet, upon the mere ipsi dixit of a political worker, this man is dismissed, and you appoint a new postmaster without knowing anything as to what his qualifications are. In pursuing this course you are making a great deal of trouble for yourself, as is evidenced in the case of St. Charles de Caplan. The result is that everyone who has been dismissed becomes aggravated in his feelings against the Government of the day, and numerous applicants for the vacant office have to be dealt with. One man is appointed, and a dozen are dissatisfied. The party in power loses more than it gains by the change, whereas we get more partisans in the next election. Both political parties would do well, unless it is a flagrant case, to consider first the public interest, guided by a reasonable opinion of the people of the locality.

There are one or two
matters that I wish to bring to the attention of the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier). I do not think I have any fault to find with the Postmaster General for dismissing public servants, who, after thorough and fair investigation, have been convicted of active political partisanship. There may be faults in the system, but I am not going to offer any criticism of the Postmaster General, or the head of any other department, who takes the ground that a man who has been an active partisan while holding a public office, should, after full investigation, be dismissed. But there are instances where the partisan doctrine is carried to a very great extreme, and I have one or two of these instances in connection with the administration of the Post Office Department by the present head of the department that I want to bring to his notice at the present moment. I think I can prove that in these instances the Postmaster General went very far afield to show that his appointments, and the administration of his department, were far' more in the interest of the party to which he belongs than in the interest of the public whom the Post Office Department is supposed to serve.
A little over a year ago, in the little village named Wakaw, in my constituency, which is on a new railway being built M. MAIfCIL (Bonarenture).
from Young, on the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific to Prince Albert, a change of postmasters was considered desirable. It was brought to the attention of the Postmaster General that an appointment should be made, a.s the situation of the old postoffice was some distance out of the village, and it was necessary in the interest of the public that the post office should be moved into the village and another person appointed as postmaster. On the 21st February, 1912, a widow woman, who was a restaurant or boarding-house keeper, an estimable person, who was supporting a small family by her own efforts, and an lived in this village, made application to the Postmaster General to be appointed as postmistress. Accompanying her Tequest was a petition of fifty-one residents, which number, in that place, practically included all the residents, comprising the reeve, or mayor, or overseer, the president of the board of trade, the banker and the business men of the place. This application was made in February, 1912. According to the custom of the department, the gentleman who was the Conservative candidate in the last election in that constituency was appealed to for a recommendation. I refer to Mr. Harvey Hearn, a lawyer of the village of Wadena, in the constituency of Humboldt. Mr. Hearn was informed of Mrs. Gould's request, and of the petition which had been sent in her favour. The minister will have no trouble in looking up the facts in connection with this matter, because, pursuant to an Order of the Senate, dated February 12, 1913, a return was brought down of all papers, telegrams, petitions, letters and other documents in the case, and it is from that return that I take the information which I have at the present time, along with complaints that I received last year from the residents of the place in reference to the appointment. It seems however, that Mr. Hearn changed his mind very shortly after he had recommended Mrs. Gould by his letter of April 11, 1912. He had received some new light on the situation in this village, and on the 29th April he wrote recommending the appointment of a man by the name of McCloskey, who was a school teacher some few miles out of Wakaw, but who, it was understood, was going to live in that village. Within two or three weeks, this Mr. Hearn changed his mind about his recommendation of Mrs. Gould, and decided to recommend this man by the name of McCloskey. In a very short time the citizens of the village became aware of this prospective change. On May 21, 1912, the board of trade sent in a very strong protest against the appointment of Mr. McCloskey as not being a fit person for the position of postmaster. Immediately after that, the de-

partment wired the inspector to suspend the appointment of Mr. MeCloskey until an investigation could be made as to his fitness for office. On the 29th of May the department wrote Mr. Hearn, the Conservative candidate in the last election in that constituency, notifying him of the protest of the board of trade. On the 21st of May, a petition signed by practically all the citizens of the village, was sent to the department, protesting against Mr. Mc-Closkey's appointment. Following the instructions of the Postmaster General, the inspector at Saskatoon investigated the matter. On the file is the reply from the assistant to the inspector at Saskatoon, in which he declared that very serious charges of a personal nature, affecting Mr. Me-Cioskey's conduct when teaching in a school in the neighbourhood and as to his personal conduct in and around the village during his term of residence there, had been made to the inspector by letter and otherwise by the people of the village. The department notified Mr. Hearn of the inspector's report and of the protests of the_ citizens. On the 15th of June another petition was sent in for the appointment of Mrs. Gould.

speechtext: I understand that the Postmaster General is not anxious to go on with these estimates at the present moment. If that is the case, I can defer any remarks I have to make.	-

I am informed that the Postmaster General is not feeling too well. We might perhaps adjourn the consideration of his estimates; take up the Department of Railways, and I presume by tomorrow my hon. friend will be able to go on with his estimates.

Perhaps to-morrow
afternoon or evening. I have been somewhat under the weather for a few days.

We are glad to allow the Postmaster General to go home. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) will not be here to-morrow. If the estimates go on to-morrow, we can keep an item so that he can make his remarks.
Certainly.
With the consent of the committee we might say that civil government estimates are passed, with the understanding that we earn discuss them again.

I am quite willing that the discussion should go on later. I must thank my hon. friends opposite for their consideration.
The hon. member for Rouville has asked several times about the Parcel Post Bill. If, as I understand it, the matter is not controversial, I am prepared to put this Bill through at any time. To-night, newspapers on both sides of politics in Ottawa,
say that the Bill has disappeared from the Order Paper. If they will look at Order Vo. 21, they will see that the Bill has not disappeared. Any controversial Bill, which would be likely to keep us here much longer, although we enjoy the company of our hon. friends, would have to be discarded, but anything not controversial-
We would have to read the Bill first.
I am sure my hon. friends will have plenty of time to read the Bill.
Can the hon. Postmaster General let us see the Bill ? At present we cannot say whether it is controversial or not.

The Bill has been
printed for fifteen days or three weeks and I think my hon. friends will find it on their files. It is Bill No. 210.
Railways and Canals-capital-Trent canal construction, $1,000,000.

When the House rose at six o'clock, several hon. members had expressed their views on this waterway. My hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) rather thought the work had not been progressing with sufficient rapidity. It is perhaps the oldest work in Canada that has been kept almost continuously under construction. I think he will admit that during the last two or three years a great deal of work has been done in developing this waterway. He will find that, in the Department of Railways and Canals, resolutions of the board of trade and the city-council of Peterborough, as well as other councils on the line of the canal, speaking very favourably of the progress of the work. Now, I think a wrong impression was left on the minds of some hon. gentlemen as to the canal not being 'opened up '-that being the term used. It is true, the canal is not yet completed to either lake Ontario or Georgian bay, but it has been open for navigation for many years. One can take a steamer at Peterborough and go to any point on lake Simcoe. I agree with my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) that this is a very beautiful route, in fact I think I am safe in saying that on this continent there is no more picturesque route than this Trent canal. I have made the trip, and know whereof I speak. It is really an eyeopener to one who makes it for the first time. Lake after lake is crossed and the most beautiful scenery brought into view, scenery that has lost none of its natural charm. I advise the members of this House and the people of Canada and elsewhere, if they want a really beautiful and rest-giving trip to

take this tour from Peterborough through to lake Simcoe.
A good many questions were asked today about the land damages. These come about in this way: Dams have to be constructed for the conservation of the water, and naturally, where the waters are raised, lands are overflowed . It takes a long time to get all these claims settled, especially when, as the work proceeds and other dams are built, new claims arise. It is not an easy matter to deal with them, all- it is a task that is perhaps not so difficult as tedious. I believe about $274,000 has been spent in land damages, and it will be some time before these cases are all concluded. Originally the dams on this system belonged to and were maintained by the Ontario Government to facilitate the operations of lumbermen. The provincial government collected timber dues, and in return, maintained dams that the lumbermen might have water to float their logs. Under an arrangement, made I think, in 1908, these dams were transferred to the Dominion authority, and the Dominion since that time has proceeded with the work, and has constructed good dams and bridges as well as building the canal. A question of jurisdiction arose between the provincial authorities and the Dominion. When my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, who is now with us, was against us on this matter- when he was in the Ontario Government- he with his colleagues rather maintained that these water-powers and the waters on this route belonged to the provincial government, and that the Dominion should hand over to the province the leases made for water-power. That is largely a legal question. I maintained on behalf of the Dominion Government that the ownership of these water-powers was vested in the federal authority and proceeded on that line. Certain arrangements were made with a company to develop power along the Trent system. There were a great many smaller leaseholders, some of the original patents having been granted a century or so ago, and arrangements had to be made with these holders, which arrangements were amicably made in most cases. The ownership was thus vested in the company, which proceeded to develop the power. I think the result of that was good, as along that line and within striking distance of it, very cheap power was obtained and is being obtained. Hon. members who were in the House then will recall that it was in connection with this power that the first Act was introduced to give the Railway Commissioners the power to regulate rates. I believe we should not have had the HydroElectric so early in eastern Ontario if we had not developed that power. However that might be controversial, and I am not seeking to raise any controversy now.
Mr. GRAHAM.
Could the minister tell us what horse-poweiv has been developed along the Trent canal? Could he tell us also how many towns are being served by the Seymour Power Company? Thirdly, have arrangements been made with the manufacturers in the town of Campbellford, which arrangements were under way, I think, at the time of the change of government? Fourthly, what is the case that was stated to the Exchequer Court? I might explain that in order to settle the difference between the provincial and the federal authority as to the proprietorship of the water-powers along the canal a case has been submitted to the Exchequer Court.

I think the province
of Ontario has filed a case, but no answer has been put in yet.

They have asked for a
fiat?

Yes. It would not be for the Trent alone. The position taken by the Ontario Government, as I understand it, is that the water belongs to the province, the federal authority having the right to control it for navigation purposes; -that before it goes into the canal and after it flows out, whether through the mouth or otherwise, it belongs to the province.

The case would be a
general cne?
Yes, to settle the question forever.

I think that when the
hon. minister's legal branch, or the Justice Department, take up the preparation of their reply, they will find that there are special circumstances connected with the Trent and special Acts that do not apply perhaps to any other stream in Ontario. I assume that my hon. friend will put in the strongest case he can on behalf [DOT] of the federal authority
I think yoii can depend on the Justice Department in such a matter.

Because my own view- of course this is a legal matter on which I do not speak with authority-is that the province has no good ground so far as the Trent is concerned, whatever may be the truth about other waters. Can the minister give me the other information I asked for?

I have no memorandum before me of the. number of towns served by the Seymour Power Company or how much power is developed. The Campbellford situation has not yet been cleaned up. I went there last year and tried to make a settlement but I thought * they wanted too much.
I thought that myself.

What will be done, I do not know, but I will try to make a settlement. In reference to the Trent, whatever may be the decision of the court, the Seymour Power Company, which has vested interests there, must be protected, and I think the Government should see that it is protected.

I think that one large
insurance company has invested quite a large sum of money in that locality. I do not think anything should be done to deprive them of their vested rights, but I have strong views on the rights of the Dominion, particularly on that route. I shall be quite satisfied if my hon. friend will get me that information.
I will, with pleasure.

As one of the humble
members from the Trent district, I have been reproached for not giving the Opposition full credit for the efforts they have made on behalf of the Trent canal. Let me say that I thoroughly appreciate, and we all thoroughly appreciate, the energetic efforts made by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and those who assisted him in the matter, and that we are very grateful indeed for the thorough appreciation he has shown of all aspects of the Trent Valley canal.

I also desire to add a word along that line. For ten or eleven long years after the Liberal party came into office, not very much was done on the canal, but I want to compliment the hon. member for South Renfrew for what he did, after he took hold of matters, to pass the work on as rapidly as he could.

In reference to the
Welland canal, has there been a final decision reached as to the crossing of the Welland river by the canal at the town of Welland? Are the canal and the river to be brought to the same level, or is the canal to be carried over the river, or the river under the canal?

The engineers recommend turning the river into the canal. If that be done, while I do not think we are legally bound to help the different towns along the route, I think we would do so. I think we would save money, and help the towns out too, by bringing the water supply from the lake. It would be a long route, but I think we can do it and save money.

You will without doubt have a better canal by doing it that way. I am quite willing to accept, as I am sure the minister will accept, the opinion of the
engineers. Has there been a final decision arrived at?
We want to hear from the towns before we make a final decision, although it is not a matter that must be settled before we call for tenders.

Do I understand that
tenders will be advertised for the carrying on of the work?

The advertisements
will be out by Monday.

I wish to remind the minister of the St. Peter's canal. This is . the only canal we have in the maritime provinces, and although it is not very large, to us^ in the island of Cape Breton it is a very important one. The minister is aware that a certain amount of money was set apart two years ago for the enlargement of the St. Peter's canal. The improvement and enlargement of the canal is particularly important for shipping from east to west, that is from the Bras d'Or lakes and from the coal mines in the eastern part of the island. I understand that the work is proceeding very slowly, and I would like to find out from the minister how much time the contractor still has. for its completion, and what are the prospects of finishing the work within the time mentioned in the contract. If itis not to be finished within the time mentioned in the contract, when may we hope that it will be completed?
I wish to urge again upon the minister the necessity of having that work completed at the earliest possible time. We have two large quarries on the Bras d'Or lake, and the product of those quarries would go through the canal if it were sufficiently large to accommodate the vessels. I understand that when the canal is completed it will be large enough to allow these vessels to go through, but in its present condition, they cannot do so. My hon. friend will therefore understand that the prompt completion of this work is highlv important.

The contractor was to have finished the work by next year, but the engineer says he does not think it will be completed until the spring of 1915. I will, however, take note of what the hon. member says, and endeavour to bring the work to completion at as early a date as possible.
Can my hon. friend give me any idea as to the route which has been decided on for the Welland canal?

The route will follow the valley of Ten Mile creek from lake Ontario, crossing the present canal below lock No. 11 at the level which now exists there, the rise having been effected* by three isolated locks with suitable pondage

areas intervening. This level is carried through to the foot of the escapement below Thorold, which is overcome by three locks in flight and a single lock on the upper level, in the town of Xnorold. Beyondj Thorold the level of low water in lake Erie will be held to Port Colborne, the present canal route being generally followed except between Port Robinson and Welland where it is proposed to utilize the Welland river and at a noint near Humberstone wheTe the present sharp bend will be done away with by a cut-off. The guard lock will 'be built in this cut-off and will he utilized to protect the canal from high water of lake Erie.
Will there be any further question as to the lowering of the level of the water of lake Erie?
No.
How much of the old canal is being used?
Nineteen miles out of the twenty-seven.
How many locks will there be in the whole system? We have now twenty-seven.
We w'ill have seven.
That will be a vast improvement. By this route we have none of those immense looks that were spoken of?

Each one will be
forty-six and a half feet.
How long, how wide, and how deep will they be?
Eight hundred feet clear of openings, eighty feet wide and with thirty feet depth on the sills.
The locks will be built for thirty feet, but the canal will not be built for thirty feet at present?
No, it would be no use doing that until the Sault is built to a depth of thirty feet.

The scheme will be to build the locks eight hundred feet by eighty feet with capacity for thirty feet draft, but the canal at present will not be built with a draft of thirty feet. Later on, if it is thought desirable to increase the depth to thirty feet, the canal can be built to that depth without any new locks. Thirty feet on the sills will take a steamer that will draw a little more than that. You can see that at the Sault any day. Could my hon. friend tell me what his estimate is for the completion of the canal?
Mr. COCHRANE.
Have the engineers given a fairly approximate estimate of the time it will take to complete it?
Five years.
It will have to go fairly rapidly. $2,000,000 would only be $10,000,000 expended in five years.
I thought that would be all we would get out this year.
Where are the contracts to be given out this year, and what are they for?

They will start in
at lake Ontario, and we will advertise section after section so as to have them come in a little later on.
Why could not all tire sections be advertised together?
Not at once, we will have section 1 advertised now and then section 2, and so on, so that contractors if they do not get one contract will have a chance at the others.
The intention is to advertise section 1 at present?	.
The others will come in a few days after.

The minister suggested
that there would probably be a conference with the various municipalities who are using water at present from the canal. That would mean Welland, Thorold, Merri-ton, and St. Catherines. I presume there will be a conference as to the proportionate part of the cost which each of these municipalities should pay to procure fresh water from lake Erie in the construction of the large pipe line contemplated.
Yes.

And if that conference
does result in a satisfactory arrangement between the department and these municipalities you will put the canal and the river on the same level from Welland to Port. Robinson, but assuming that those conferences do not come to a satisfactory conclusion?
I do not think we are legally bound to do it. I think it would be better for the towns, they would get far better water than they are getting out of the canals.
The towns will not want to pay very much.

Oh yes.
Mr. 'GERMAN:	There will be an election on before the canal is built and there is a lot of difficulty ahead. I do not want to say anything to criticize the problem a

bit and anything I can do to help the minister I shall do [DOT]with great pleasure
Thank you.

-and take my share of the responsibility of getting it settled up because I know the difficulty in the situation. I want to see it settled to the best advantage of the locality and of the department and, as far as I can aid in getting it settled without difficulty, I will certainly use my best endeavours to do so.
I suppose that damming the river will create quite a lot of land damages.
Quite a bit I suppose.

Has the minister
thought about how much water power there is there now and how much there will be when the new canal is constructed?

I do not know that
we should do much in water-power in the new canal. We are building that canal for navigation and while we could probably make some money out of it, I think we would certainly interfere with the effectiveness of the canal and navigation if we did. I cannot give the amount of water-power there because I never had it figured out, and there are so many old leases that you cannot do much with unless you expropriate them.

They are hoary with age and have antiquated histories. They were got for nothing in the first place. It is hard work to get the money out of them. The powers on the old Weliand canal will-not be particularly affected but, as the minister has very rightly said, the water-power must be kept secondary to the navigation. We hear a great deal of discussion in the House about how much water-power will be developed on this or that Government undertaking. It is very easy to practically spoil the value of a large public expenditure in endeavouring to get a comparatively small income, because once the current in a canal exceeds a certain speed you very rnuoh interfere with navigation. I would take the view that the minister does; I would make no promise at all about waterpower and then I would see that the water-powers were used sparingly so as not to interfere with navigation.

Everyone is pleased that the minister is building for the future and that the locks will be of sufficient length to allow large ships to pass up. I understand that the new locks on the canal will be 800 feet.
That is, there will be room for a boat 800 feet long.
Must we wait until the whole -work is completed before we can get a boat of that length through the locks? I understand that at present no ship longer than 270 odd feet can pass.

We will have to wait until the canal is finished.
Enlarging Port Colborne elevator, $150,000.

Will $150,000 build the
addition to the elevator and make it the size it was originally intended to be?
Yes, it will bring the capacity up to 2,000,000 bushels. The foundation was in before.
Will it be completed this summer, and be ready for the fall?
It will be ready for the fall grain.
Has it been a success? How much grain has gone through?

It is a success all
right. Last year it was $18,000 ahead, I think, and this year it is $22,000 ahead.

How many bushels of
grain went through?

Up to the 31st of October, 1912, the elevator handled 9,653,343 bushels, and for the year 1911, from January 1 to December 31, it handled
7,000,000 bushels. I think we should have more elevator room at Montreal. I do not think we have enough to keep boats loading and trains unloading quickly.
That is evident.
Should the harbour faciE ities in Montreal not be increased too?
They have done good work in the past and they are doing good work now, but I feel we ought to have the elevator room increased very much.
And more harbour space?
They will have room for 6,000,000 bushels in Montreal this year, which is a great deal more than they have had hitherto.
Of what use in the transportation of grain was this elevator at Port Colborne?
The larger boats that could not go through the canal unloaded there.
Was that done with the whole of the grain?
Not all, some of the boats went through all the way.

Was it a case of the elevator being used to discharge the big vessels so that smaller vessels could take the

grain from that elevator to Montreal, or was there some lightering of some of the big vessels going through the canal?
Both.

I think a few minutes
would not be 'badly spent discussing the question that the hon. member for Edmonton has suggested. Originally it was supposed that the Welland canal would not be enlarged and that the large boats would discharge their cargo at Bort Colbome, and that from Port Coiborne to Montreal there would be a line of barges or boats of full canal size, carrying the grain from PoTt Colbome to Montreal. At one tim&I thought that that was a feasible proposition, and I am not so certain now that it is not. However, it was thought advisable to enlarge the Welland canal, thereby allowing the large upper lake freighters, carrying 300,000 bushels of wheat, to go through the Welland canal, to pass as faT down as Prescott and to discharge their cargo there, the wheat being carried in barges from that point to Montreal. The Welland canal project having been embarked upon, I have been of opinion, and am still, that the Government should proceed to enlarge the St. Lawrence route from Prescott to Montreal, and make the depth thirty feet from Port Arthur^ to Montreal, so as to allow a ship carrying
300,000	bushels of wheat to load her cargo at Port Arthur and discharge it in Liverpool as she could do ii the whole canal system along the St. Lawrence route were completed. I believe it would be a scheme worthy of the capability of the Minister of Railways, and one that would redound to the credit of Canada. I for one would like to see that proposition adopted and carried out. During the recess the minister with his engineers, should consider whether or not they should not begin at once to enlarge the St. Lawrence route and make it equal in depth to the Welland canal so that you would have thirty feet all the way.

Does my hon. friend
anticipate that it will ever pay any vessel to carry 300,000 bushels of gram to Liverpool in competition with an ocean liner which would have its mail subvention, its passenger list, a large amount of high priced freight and which would practically carry grain as ballast?

I really cannot answer my hon. friend from East Simcoe because I 'am not sufficiently conversant with the matter. I would put the route from the great lakes to the Atlantic ocean in a position to alloiv them to do so if they wanted to. If it would not be profitable they would not do it but they could go to Montreal, discharge their cargo and return and probably that would be as much as they
would do. I doubt very much if oceangoing vessels would come into fresh water or if fresh water vessels would go into salt water. But you should provide a thirty-foot channel from the great lakes to Montreal .

The department has
given a good deal of attention to this question already. It is a question affecting international waters and therefore before any thing is done we will have to take it up with the Government of the United States.

In this matter of transportation, as in other matters, the less a man knows about it the more fluently he is able to talk about it. I do not know very much about it but I am going to put a question to the minister in connection with this large expenditure and I want to be understood as not objecting to it because it is large. All I want to know is that it will be effective. As you make your vessels larger, does it not follow that any delay of the ship, or any possible danger that may occux to her, militates against the use of the large vessel more than it does against a smaller vessel? Do you not lose, in the time you take to go through the twenty-seven locks of the Welland canal, so much in the holding of that expensive vessel that you do not make a gain in the carriage of the cargo in proportion to what you would make if it were open water?
There are only seven locks in the new canal.

I will admit that is an advantage. When you get a 300,000 bushel vessel as against a 100,000 bushel vessel; with the larger amount of capital locked up in that vessel, the larger amount of running expenses and the risk of damage in going through the canal, is it not possible that you lose as much as you gain and that the results of the enlargment of this canal will not be in proportion to its cost? I do not wish to be understood as making a statement to that affect, but from having given a little istudy to these matters it strikes me that there is such a possibility and that it is a matter that should be considered. The benefit of a canal is where the canal is merely a short link between two long stretchts of navigation, such as the Suez, Panama and Sault canals; but where the canal is made up of a series of locks there is involved in its use a serious loss [DOT]of time and a risk of damage to the vessel that will very seriously decrease the value of water 'transportation'' by the large vessels.

I do not profess to be an expert in transportation, hut the engineer tells me that the average travelling
Mr. OLIVER

speed of boats carrying 300,000 bushels of grain is about ten miles an hour. They will go through the seven locks in the canal in-ten hours, making about six miles an hour in doing so. I think, taking the overhead charges and everything, the
300,000	bushel vessel would beat any hundred thousand bushel vessel from Port Arthur down. A great deal of the expense that* these big boats sustain is entailed by lying at the dock by reason of their not being able to unload quickly enough.

There is a considerable difference of opinion as to the wisdom of making provision for heavy draught steamers. I had a man who was engaged in the carrying trade, and a very large grain dealer, on two occasions, perhaps three, demonstrate to me that it was cheaper, or fully as cheap, to bring grain to Prescott, or Kingston, in large lake vessels and reship it in smaller barges to Montreal than it would be for the larger vessels to go all the way through to Montreal. His statement was that you can take a series of barges and load them with grain at very small expense, that they hold a large amount of grain, that they can be operated cheaply, and that the larger vessel can return immediately and pick up its cargo in the cities along the lakes. A great deal of the cargo is taken from the larger cities to the West, and a large boat can get back very much more quickly by transferring its cargo to barges than if it went all the way through to Montreal and came back again. Sir AVilliam Van Horne gave the opinion at one time when he was discussing the Georgian Bay canal scheme, in which he took a very great interest, that a fourteen-foot channel for the Georgian Bay canal wrould be sufficient.

A barge canal?
Mr. GRAHAM A barge canal, and he contended that grain products could be transported _ as cheaply in these smaller barges as in larger vessels. There are many of the foremost experts on transportation who do not agree with these theories. It will take quite a bit of investigation, in so far as the deepening of the St. Lawrence canals is concerned, before the scheme is entered upon because there is such a variety of opinions as to the wisdom of enlarging the St. Lawrence canals. But there seems to be a general consensus of opinion that it is a wise thing to enlarge the Welland canal so as to bring lake navigation as close to Montreal as possible, because when you have enlarged the Welland canal you have nothing to interfere with the larger vessels going down to the head of the rapids.
Carillon and Grenville canal-lengthening . apron, Carillon dam, $12,000.

I think that it was here that a water power lease was given to a company a few years ago under the conditions that they should spend so much money within a given time. I think the rates were placed under the jurisdiction of the board of railway commissioners. Have they complied with the terms of their lease?
They have developed a very small amount of power. They are transferring their lease to another company who want to take it up and develop a larger amount of power.
It will be a success shortly?

Yes.
Cornwall canal, $56,400.

There was some question at one time as to the leasing of a certain increase of power to the Toronto Paper Mills at Cornwall. They proceeded to do some work themselves and the department did not approve of that work. Was that lease given ?
There was no extension given. The development of water power there has affected the current.
They are using practically all the water power that can be used?

That is right. It will not be increased.
Parran's Point canal-improving lower entrance, $22,000.
This is for building an entrance at the lower end.
How much will it take to finish it ?
This finishes it.
What is being built ?

We are extending the pier.
Lachine canal-filling gaps in canal walls near Brewster's bridge, $17,000.

Gap No. 1 is an entrance to the original Lachine canal which was closed in 1845. Gap No. 2 is the old abandoned slip. They are making the walls continuous.
Murray canal-removing high spots in canal and approaches, $1,000.
The Murray canal has had several wants. It needed better lighting. Has it got that ?
Not yet.

Several	deputations
waited on the department at different



times, more particularly since the cement works and the quarries were there, asking that the canal be lighted, as they claimed they could not go through the canal at night with any load.
I have not received any deputations.

Representations were
made to the Government that there were certain shoals or impediments at the east entrance that should be removed, and the Public Works Department was asked to do some dredging.
I think some work has been done there.

If it has not been done,
I think it should be done. It is more necessary than the lighting.
I will make a note of it.
Who is doing the work, and is it by contract ?

Randolph McDonald Company, by contract.
Quebec canals, $12,100.
This is the concrete facing in the dam at Valieyfield. There is a great leakage there at present. The dam is used by the power companies there and it holds up the levels of lake St. Francis.	.

Weller, son of the

Welland canal-heavy repairs, $30,000.
What are these repairs?

Renewing spillway
from hydraulic raceway No. 2 to raceway No. 3, St. Catherines; renewing six old canal weir foot-bridges in concrete; renewing wooden cover of drain near Marlatt's bridge in concrete; repairing lock gates, old canal; renewing six new canal weir footbridges in concrete; rebuilding lock destroyed by fire on east side of harbour at Port Dalhousie.
How many safety devices have been installed?

A device was installed on lock 24, and during the spring of 1912 it was the means of preventing two serious accidents. In one case a steamer entering the locks collided with the right head gate. To pay expenses in connection witn cases before the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, $15,000.
. Mr. GRAHAAI: I have always contended that the Board of Railway Commissioners was not intended to be a court where the ordinary man had to be represented by counsel. Where there are separate investigations, such as I have mentioned, it is all right because the Government side of the case has to be put forward very strongly.

Would it not be well for the Government to have a counsel to

take charge of the cases before the Railway Board as they come along and make it his whole business? Of course we have not decided on anything of that kind.

I am afraid not, it might result in a good deal of red tape. Under ordinary corcumstances the poor man can write to the secretary of the commission and get speedy justice without any frills, as it were. I discussed this matter several times with the late Justice Mabee, who pointed out that in his opinion counsel would be a nuisance, and that he would rather hear complaints from the people themselves than listen to arguments of counsel. I have no objection to this item for these larger investigations, but I would object to the appointment of counsel on general principles to look after those smaller cases, because I think the people are better served now.

I would be sorry to
-see the chairman of the commission refuse to permit anyone to plead his case, no matter how small it might be. But there are many big cases on which the Government should be represented and it struck me that it would be a good thing if we had a man studying these things all the time.
That would be representing the Government all the time. My objection was to having a man there to represent the people, to take up the cases of different people.

If you had a permanent counsel -representing the Government he would be there iu all cases continually. The result would be that an individual who had a case before the board woitld feel that his interests were not properly safeguarded, and he would not dare to go before the Railway Board unless he had a lawyer to act for him; whereas now a man with a complaint as to a crossing or anything goes to the board or communicates with the board, then if the department here feels that the public interest should he more particularly safeguarded than it can be by those looking after it all they have to do is to postpone the case and notify the_ minister and counsel can easily be appointed. I do not think it would be a wise thing to have a general counsel standing there all the time.

Mr. Chairman, on the 14th of May last, when I raised objection in this House to the increase of salary of the 'Chairman of the Railway Commissioners, I said that perhaps those commissioners were not working an hour a day. In making that assertion, I evidently fell into some exaggeration, and, in justice to those gentlemen, I must admit that they are working a little longer every Mr. COCHRANE.
day. But, while admitting that, I am not ready to accept willingly that enormous salary which we are paying to the chairman of that commission.
The Postmaster General has allowed himself, in that circumstance, to make towards me certain observations which, to say the least, were somewhat bold, and in a language which I would certainly not have used towards him. I regret that he is not now at his seat so that he might hear what I have to say in answer. He has said, amongst other things, in justification of that enormous increase of salary of the Chairman of the Railway Commissioners, that those men were giving up lucrative positions and salaries as high as $25,0(W a year to become the servants of the public. Well, now, I will say that the fact that the hon. minister says such a thing does not absolutely prove that it must be true. Moreover, and even admitting that it is true, the barristers who are getting such a salary are not lowering themselves when they accept positions in the Government service; because, from being the servants of the public, with all the worries of the suitors, and trials of all kinds, and often working 8 or 10 hours a day, they become the servants of the Government, with fixed hours for their work of four or five hours a day at the utmost, and with a nice private car at their disposition to carry them across the country, without charge whatever. And they then become independent with a fixed and assured salary, which is well worth a slight reduction of salary taken from one or the other, and that often amidst the curses of individuals who are being skinned alive. If it should be true that some advocates are able to raise such a high salary in our country, it only shows in my sense that the judicial tariffs are exorbitant and should be adjusted as soon as possible so that our courts of justice would not take undue advantage of the poor fellows who are forced to have recourse to them; because there is not a man in this country who is able to earn in the strict sense of the word $66.66 per day, while the poor labourer painfully earns $1.50 to $2 a day. I even say it is a real shame to confess such a thing, and that is with the supposition that the advocate works 300 days during the year.
If we are now supposing, as it is in reality, that he only works 200 days during the year, after deduction of vacation, legal holidays, &c., we come to a salary of $80 per day, or $13.33 per hour, if we reckon that he is in his office six hours per day, or $16 per hour if he is only there five hours.
If we now compare in the same way the salary of the Chairman of the Railway Commissioners, we come to the following figures: $12,500 per year, supposing a work of 300 days, gives $41.66 per day, or $10.46

for every hour, admitting that he works but four hours a day, and at that rate he should -work on every working day of the year.
Now, if we deduct the legal holidays, about ten each year, the Saturdays of every week, which have a half holiday, the vacations which every one of those big salaried officers always gets as a matter of course, and which are at least of thirty days every year, we find that all those superior officers are only working from 230 to 250 days per year; and calculating their salary of $12,500 a year at an average rate of 240 days of work, we find that they are getting $52.08 per day, or $13 for each one of the four hours of work they are giving, or $10.41 for each hour if they work five hours a day.
That being the case, I say it is a real shame to ask a labourer, a farmer, or any workingman to bleed themselves to death so that they may be able to pay all those exorbitant and extravagant salaries; and the people of our country will not approve that, notwithstanding the opinion of the hon. Postmaster General, of the hon. members for Rouville and Three Rivers, or some other lawyers. The Prime Minister of the country is the only one who receives such a high salary. The other ministers, who are obliged to be in their office all the year round, and to make enormous expenses so as to make in society a figure corresponding to their position; who are obliged to defray the cost of expensive elections and to condescend to meet their electors every day -and those meetings are not always pleasant-those ministers, I say, are only receiving $7,000 per year.
What kind of consideration are we bestowing, then, upon our ministers, if they are not at least worth as much as their simple employees. I say that such a state of things may be the cause of discrediting the Administration of this country, and should not be tolerated any longer.
The hon. Postmaster General has said, with a kind of extenuation of his expressions, that I did not know anything about the work of the Railway Commissioners. I very willingly forgive him that language, which must have been caused by the somewhat harsh observations I had made on the legal profession; but, after all, he admits himself that there are lawyers who are voracious enough to extort from the poor suitors from $20,000 to $25,000 a year.
In order to show to the hon. Postmaster General that he has somewhat exceeded the limits of truth, when he said that I did not know anything about the work of the Railway Commissioners, I will in the first place say to him that I have specially studied the case before speaking of it, and I have discovered the following conditions in the report for the year 1911, which has
489 pages. I have also looked for the number of complaints which those gentlemen had received in 1911. They number in all 573, and those that have been heard are 565. On that total of 565, eight have been adjourned and several have been withdrawn even before the hearing. And moreover, there were a good number of cases for which the examination is always about the same, as grade crossings and so on. Every one knows what those complaints are about; it is the same thing, with scarcely any difference, and when one of those questions has been settled the same proceedings will apply to 20 or 25 others.
For the setting up of stations on sidings, there are about 20 cases. Those cases are still easy enough to settle. The same remark applies to the determination of the locality where a station has to be built, when such questions are in dispute, and there have been a good number of complaints in that respect.
I may say that we are not lacking of jurists who have as many cases to plead every year, and they do not claim a salary of $12,000. They are satisfied with much less, four or five thousand dollars at the utmost, and they put in a good deal more work.
I may also add that the Railway Commission is not composed of only six judges; the staff comprises 77 members who are all paid by the country, and those are the ones who do the work, because we often see that the Commissioners base their decisions on the report of their engineers, without taking the trouble to visit the localities. It natur-' ally follows that those 77 members are really the ones who have been the means of deciding the greatest number of those 565 cases.
It seems to me that there is not enough work to justify such salaries, especially the one being paid to the chairman, who is receiving to-day $8,000.
He gets $10,000.

Grand Trunk Pacific railway-remuneration to Government director, $2,000.

Does this director make a report; if so, how often, and what is the information in it?
Mr. BOULAY.

The report is made
once a year, and, as before, it does not contain very much.
On one or. two occasions I laid the report before the House. It might be useful for reference.

I will do so.
Surveys and inspections-railways, $100,000.
Are any surveys projected in the maritime provinces?

I told my hon. friend one afternoon that I proposed to send a traffic man over the lines that have been proposed to get some information and to see what justification there may be for building roads, and I intend to carry out that intention.
That would come under this vote?
Yes.

Does the minister adhere to the policy he laid down last session that in the case of a new branch line of the Intercolonial he would require to be satisfied that the traffic would be sufficient to pay the interest and running expenses?

I did not Jay that
down. I referred to any branch line that would not pay running expenses without interest, a very different proposition.
Does the minister expect a railway to pay running expenses at the very commencement?

Branch lines have
been running there for some time, and they have not been able to pay running expenses up till now, and there is not very much prospect of them doing so.

To what branch lines
does the minister refer? .
I do not iefer to any particular branch line, but to what has been done in some cases.

The minister must have an eye to the traffic when he is laying out a" branch line, but I' do not altogether agree with him that he has a right to expect enough traffic at the start to pay running expenses. If that rule were applied to the other railways in Canada, there would be very few built. I do not think that that rule could have been carried out in the case of the Canadian Pacific Tailway. The traffic on that road at the commencement was not sufficient, I understand, to pay running expenses, and certainly it was not sufficient in the case of the Intercolonial. The same is true of the Grand Trunk railway. I think the minister ex-

pects a little too much. If the traffic is there, it is possible to develop it.
That is the information I want to get.

It might take some
time to develop traffic. In Eastern Nova Scotia he will find a certain amount of traffic right at his hand, such as the carrying of wood to the market, but there are other kinds of traffic that might be developed in time. He cannot expect that they would be developed just as quickly as the road was built. I hope he will not look at this matter from too narrow a point of view. We are assisting transportation to a very large extent in other parts of Canada, and why not in eastern Canada? I think we ought to deal with it in the same way as we do in western and central Canada. We ought to loiok to the future, and, if a traffic is likely to be developed, give railway facilities.
Mr. McKENZIE- The minister says he proposes to send a traffic man over those roads. Does he include in that statement the different roads in Nova Scotia, that we had under consideration?
Yes.
I hope he will send a good man.
We will talk it over together.

Perhaps the better way would be to send an engineer and a traffic manager to have them strike an average.
Railways and canals-collection of revenue -Intercolonial railway, $13,000,000.
That is the working expenses of the. Intercolonial railway ?
Yes.

We discussed a good many of the matters connected with the working expenses. There is an increase on the Windsor branch. I suppose the reason for that is really the same as the reason for the increase on the Intercolonial, that is increase in traffic ?
Yes.
What is the deficit on the Prince Edward Island railway ?
I know that for April [DOT] it was $14,000.
I have always taken the ground that the Prince Edward Island railway will never show a balance on the right side as long as it is run as a separate entity.

No, but I think that when we get the ferry across and put a
live man in there, it will make a difference.

It will make a difference with your freight traffic and with your passenger traffic as well. A great many people who are selling tickets in Prince Edward Island now might be able to sell them for the Intercolonial railway.
That is right. I have not the statement of the deficit on the Prince Edward Island railway, but I can get it for the hon. gentleman.
Does the minister keep the books on the Intercolonial railway in such a way that he can tell the profit on each division of the road ?
There are four divisions of the Intercolonial railway; we are going to apply that system this year and we hope to be able to tell that when we meet the House again.

I think that possibly in establishing freight rates on the Prince Edward Island railway, the local conditions are not taken fully into consideration. The hauls there are comparatively shorter than on the mainland and the rates are so high that the railway is losing a good deal of the package business and light freight. Where hauls are short it really pays to carry the freight by teams rather than to send it by the railway. The cars are running anyway, the men are employed, and they might as well have more business to do. I speak of this from personal experience. The rates were raised lately with the object, no doubt, of reducing the deficit, but I think that possibly it will have the opposite effect, because the farmers and others doing business there will team more of their traffic and that business will be lost to the railway. I have a branch store seven or eight miles from the town of Souris and we found that even under the old rates it was cheaper to team small package freight than to send it by the railway. Of course we found it cheaper to send heavy goods, such as molasses, iron, salt, and things 'of that kind, by the railway. But, under the old rates, the difference was so small that we generally sent everything by the railway. Now that the rates have been raised, we will send all the small stuff by team, and it is a question whether the raise in the rates will have the effect of increasing the earning power of the road. It is possible that when these rates are considered by men living on the mainland, where the average haulage is much longer, the difference in the conditions is not fully taken into account. If the minister has an opportunity of discussing this matter with his officers at any time, it would be well to take that feature of the question into consideration.

Canals-staff and repairs, $1,327,630.

The two tugs that yon ordered in Montreal only came in this spring, then there is the new dredge, and the extra amount on the Welland canal is $7,000.
Canale-statistical officers, $42,500.
Can my hon. friend tell us who the statistical officer is at Cardinal, when he was appointed and whom he succeeded?
Mr. Reid is the statistical officer and he succeeded Dr. Williams.
What relation would he be to the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid)?
I think he is a brother.
Whom did he succeed?
Dr. Williams.

This is one of the things that is hardly defensible. Of course, the recommendation would be made by the Minister of Customs, as it is in his constituency. If it were in some other constituency it might be different, but it comes right home because here is a man dismissed from office and the office given to the brother of a member of the Government on the recommendation of his brother.
Mr. Reid was dismissed in 1896.

I am not going to discuss the situation, but I can if my hon. friend desires it at some other time. I just leave it to the minister himself to say whether, if he were in that position, he would think it a proper thing to do. It is rather an unusual thing to recommend your own brother in your own constituency.
I know, but there is this fact to be considered, that he was justly or unjustly dismissed in 1896, and lie thought it was only his right to be reinstated.

What are the salaries of these officers?
Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.).

Does the minister lay that
down as a principle that, if a man is dismissed by one government, he should be reinstated as soon as the other government comes in?

He had no investigation. We do not know whether he was dismissed with or without cause.
Salaries and contingencies, $180,312.50.
The changes are just the regular increases and one or two provisions for new men whom we must take in.
In what branch?

The engineering
branch, surveys.

I hope the minister will be able to find young men in Canada for these new positions. There is a general feeling that our young men do not get a fair chance in connection with the Intercolonial railway, especially in regard to promotion.
Do you mean that the engineers do not get fair play?

I am not specially referring to them; but it often happens that we have to import men from abroad to fill the highest positions in connection with the road, when we ought to promote our own employees. This road has been running ever since Confederation, and we have produced on it a very high class of men. Many of them have gone to the United States, and I am told that a large number of roads in the United States are managed by men who were produced on the Intercolonial. There must be some defect in the management or in the promotion, or we would be able to find men at home to put in these responsible positions. I think the minister is in sympathy with my view, but I do not think it has been impressed upon the Government in the past as it ought to have been. If the minister will look into the matter, he will find many bright men in his own employ; and, if he gives them a chance of promotion, he will be able to fill the most important places with Canadians produced right on the line.
